questions.question: A layer record declares: rank d = 1; one dimension with extent 250 and tile extent 40; channel layout = planar; channel count C = 3; index_encoding = 1 (raw-segmented). What is this layer's entry_count, and what is the resulting extent_length (in bytes) of its tile-index region?
questions.answer_form: Two integers: entry_count, then extent_length in bytes.
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the ceiling-division grid-count rule, the layout-dependent addressed-tile-count formula (C·N for planar vs. N for interleaved), and the index-region byte-length formula entry_count×20 + ⌈entry_count/2¹⁶⌉×4; getting any one piece wrong yields a wrong extent_length that two implementations would disagree about.

questions.question: A TARN file's first commit produces the smallest possible conforming file. The file then undergoes a second commit (its second generation). What is the smallest possible value the second commit's trailer can carry in committed_file_length?
questions.sections: §5.1/§21.2 F5 (128-byte minimum), §9.2 (commit protocol and its second Note), §6.2 (dir_offset/dir_length/trailer floors)
questions.answer_form: A single integer (bytes).
questions.why_it_matters: Requires combining the 128-byte floor for the smallest conforming file with §9.2's derivation that each commit's new F is at least the prior F plus 128 — a rule stated only in a Note that reasons from the commit protocol's own steps, not read off any table.

questions.question: A file's directory contains two layer records. Each record's name field lies entirely within that record's inline_length (so each contributes a name to the namespace), but neither name field, taken as bytes, is well-formed UTF-8. The two name fields are byte-for-byte identical to each other. Is this combination a duplicate-layer-name violation under this specification, and if so, what is its outcome class and owning scope?
questions.answer_form: State yes or no, then the outcome class and scope (e.g. "reject-file" / "file") if yes.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests whether an implementer realizes uniqueness is decided over raw bytes before validity is checked at all — the document states explicitly that two invalid names can still be "the" duplicate, a rule a reader could easily miss by validating names before comparing them.

questions.question: A remote reader opens a TARN file over a transport that services range requests but never discloses a range response's complete resource length (so the reader cannot learn the transport-authoritative file size F from the response to its trailer-suffix fetch). The reader does not use speculative suffix-window containment. Under this specification's remote-open accounting, what is the minimum total number of HTTP-style requests this reader's open requires?
questions.answer_form: A single integer (request count).
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the baseline two-request accounting (trailer suffix + directory) with the explicit carve-out for a transport that doesn't disclose complete length, which forces a separate size probe — a reader that doesn't realize this needs a third request will mis-implement ‘transport-authoritative size’ and may compare F against the wrong value.

questions.question: A reader is partway through serving a multi-entry tile-read request against one layer. It has already returned some values from this layer under this request earlier in the same session. It then encounters an index-chain failure (a segment CRC or crc_of_crc_array mismatch) while resolving a later entry needed by the same or a subsequent request against that layer. (a) What reader outcome and owning scope does this failure take — tile or layer? (b) Do the values already returned from this layer stand, or are they retroactively invalidated?
questions.answer_form: (a) one of "reject-tile" or "reject-layer"; (b) "stand" or "invalidated".
questions.why_it_matters: The specification explicitly flags this as a case where the outcome's scope (layer) differs from its detection point (tile use) — ‘although’ is the operative word — and separately states the bar is prospective only, so a reader that gets either half wrong will either over-reject already-served data or under-reject the rest of the layer.

questions.question: A layer stored at least one tile in the generation a commit supersedes. In that single commit, the writer: (i) shortens the layer's planar channel list by removing its last channel; (ii) grows one dimension's extent; and (iii) renames the layer. No other declaration changes, and every resulting declaration satisfies every bound it is subject to. Is this single commit permitted under this specification's append rules, or does it require two commits or a rewrite?
questions.sections: §20.3 step 4 (declaration-change rules for a layer that stored a tile)
questions.answer_form: "Permitted in one commit" or "requires two commits or a rewrite".
questions.why_it_matters: The governing rule's only express exception bars combining an extension and a shortening of one channel list in the same commit — it says nothing against combining a shortening with an extent growth and a rename. A question-writer or answerer who over-reads the exception as barring any combination of listed changes gets this wrong.

questions.question: A writer emits a top-level record whose type field is 0x0050 (inside the reserved range 0x0003–0x7FFF) with MUST_UNDERSTAND (flags bit 0) set to 0. Is emitting this record a file-conformance violation under this specification? If it is, which actor is assigned to detect it — reader or verifier — and does a conforming reader's processing of this record change in any way from how it would process an ordinary unknown record with MU = 0?
questions.sections: §21.2 F35 vs. F36, §10.2 (reserved vs. experimental ranges), [R-CNT-15]
questions.answer_form: Yes/no for the violation question, then the detecting actor, then yes/no for the reader-behavior-change question.
questions.why_it_matters: F36 states the reserved-range emission is a violation ‘whatever its MU bit’ — a quantifier that makes this true even at MU = 0, where no reader-visible rejection follows and only a verifier can find the defect; conflating this with F35 (which requires MU = 1) or assuming MU = 0 makes it harmless produces the wrong answer on both sub-questions.

questions.question: A record carries a type value from the experimental range (≥ 0x8000) with MUST_UNDERSTAND (flags bit 0) set to 1. State the reader's required outcome and whether the file remains conforming in each of two cases: (a) the record is a top-level record in the directory; (b) the record is a sub-record of a layer record.
questions.sections: §21.6 (closing paragraphs on "conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses"), [R-CNT-15], [R-CNT-18]
questions.answer_form: For each of (a) and (b): the reader's required outcome (e.g. reject-file or reject-layer) and "conforming" or "nonconforming".
questions.why_it_matters: The document calls this qualifier ‘load-bearing’: at top level the reader must refuse the whole file even though the file is conforming, while as a layer sub-record the same type and same MU bit yields only a layer-scoped refusal and is ‘never a ground to refuse the file’ — a distinction easy to collapse into a single rule for ‘unknown MU=1 record’.

questions.question: A planar layer has 6 channels and two dimensions declared in order (y, x) with grid counts (G_y, G_x) = (5, 5), giving N = 25 spatial tiles. What is the disk tile ordinal — the index into the layer's tile-index entry array — of the tile carrying channel index 4 (0-based) at tile coordinates (t_y, t_x) = (3, 2)?
questions.sections: §11.4 (linearization: spatial tile ordinal and disk tile ordinal formulas, [R-GEO-06])
questions.answer_form: A single integer.
questions.why_it_matters: Requires correctly composing the spatial-tile-ordinal formula (which depends on declared dimension order) with the planar disk-ordinal formula c·N + s; swapping the dimension order or misapplying the channel-major grouping yields a different, equally plausible-looking wrong integer.

questions.question: A layer has extents (E_y, E_x) = (7, 10) and tile extents (T_y, T_x) = (3, 4). Of the 12 sample positions in the tile at tile coordinates (t_y, t_x) = (2, 2) (the grid's high corner along both axes), how many are padding positions — i.e., not part of the reference array?
questions.answer_form: A single integer (count of padding positions, 0–12).
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing the grid count per axis, locating the specific high-corner tile, and counting real vs. padding positions along each axis independently before multiplying — a single arithmetic slip (e.g. using ceiling division incorrectly, or padding only one axis) produces a wrong count that would make two implementations disagree about which bytes of that tile matter.

questions.question: An interleaved layer declares two channels in order: first "mask" (type uint8, fill byte 0x01), then "val" (type float32, fill 0x7FC00000). A particular tile of this layer is addressed but its tile-index entry is the sentinel. For any one in-tile sample position, what are the decoded sample's bytes, in order, as hex?
questions.sections: §13.3 (unstored tiles read as fill, [R-TYP-08]), §14.2 (interleaved byte layout and channel order)
questions.answer_form: A sequence of hex bytes (5 bytes total), uppercase, space-separated.
questions.why_it_matters: Combines the fill-value rule (every carried channel reads as its own recorded fill, in declared channel order) with the interleaved byte-layout rule (each sample's channel values packed adjacently, numeric little-endian) — getting the channel order or either fill encoding wrong changes the byte sequence two implementations would disagree on.

questions.question: A planar tile of a uint16 channel has three decoded (unfiltered) values, in order: 0x1234, 0x5678, 0x9ABC. Under this specification's byte-shuffle filter, what are the resulting six stored (filtered) bytes, in order, as hex?
questions.sections: §17.3 (the byte-shuffle filter definition and its offset formula i·n+j), §14.2 (little-endian numeric byte encoding)
questions.answer_form: A sequence of 6 hex bytes, uppercase, space-separated, in stored order.
questions.why_it_matters: Requires correctly encoding each 16-bit value little-endian, grouping into shuffle groups of stride s=2, and placing byte i of group j at offset i·n+j rather than the more intuitive-but-wrong j·n+i or a per-value (not per-byte) permutation — the rule applied to a planar (not the document's own interleaved-example) case.

questions.question: Under this specification's bfloat16 definition, what are the two stored bytes, in little-endian order and as uppercase hex, that encode the value −2.5?
questions.sections: §12.1 (bfloat16 definition: identification with the high 16 bits of the binary32 encoding), §4.1 (little-endian byte order)
questions.answer_form: Two hex bytes, uppercase, space-separated, in stored (little-endian) order.
questions.why_it_matters: Requires deriving the IEEE 754 binary32 bit pattern of −2.5, taking its high 16 bits per the bfloat16 rule, then re-expressing that 16-bit pattern in little-endian stored byte order — three independent steps where an error in any one (sign bit, truncation point, or byte order) yields a wrong but plausible two-byte answer.

questions.question: A layer declares: rank d = 2; tile extents (20000, 20000); one channel of type float64 (element size 8 bytes); codec = 4 (lz4). Its two dimensions have declared extents (0, 50000) — i.e., one dimension's extent is 0. Is this layer's codec declaration conforming under this specification? Answer yes or no, and give the layer's addressed-tile count that determines the answer.
questions.sections: §17.2 codec 4 / [R-COD-07] (lz4 decoded-size cap, quantified over addressed tiles), §11.2 (grid count and addressed-tile count), §21.6 (zero-extent layers as a defined non-violation)
questions.answer_form: "Yes" or "No", followed by a single integer (the addressed-tile count).
questions.why_it_matters: The lz4 cap (0x7E000000 bytes) is explicitly quantified over a layer's *addressed* tiles, not its declared tile shape; this layer's tile shape alone would badly exceed the cap, but a zero-extent dimension drives its grid count, and hence its addressed-tile count, to zero — a quantifier that a reader who checks only the tile-shape arithmetic will miss, wrongly rejecting a conforming declaration.

questions.question: A layer declares a slab with run length S and slab alignment A_slab. Within one slab run, one tile's index entry has offset and length values fully consistent with ordinary packing (its offset equals the previous stored tile's offset plus that previous tile's length), but the bytes at that tile's stored extent fail the entry's own CRC-32C check. For purposes of the slab run-continuity invariant, is this entry's offset/length pair treated as transparent (skipped, the way a sentinel entry is), or as an ordinary stored tile's values that the packing relation must read normally?
questions.sections: §15.3 (entry validity — the structural vs. crc-only distinction, [R-IDX-03]), §16.2 (slab run continuity, [R-SLB-03])
questions.answer_form: "Transparent" or "ordinary (not transparent)".
questions.why_it_matters: The specification draws a sharp line between an entry that is structurally malformed (which contributes no stored extent and is transparent to run continuity, like a sentinel) and one that is well-formed but whose referenced bytes merely fail their CRC (which keeps its place and whose offset/length values the packing relation reads like any other stored tile's) — collapsing this distinction is the single most common way to mis-verify slab continuity.

questions.question: For a conforming TARN file whose trailer declares dir_offset = 16 and dir_length = 20, what is the minimum value committed_file_length (F) can take, consistent with every trailer field constraint in §6.2 and the file-size floor of §5.1/§21.2? Answer as an integer number of bytes.
questions.answer_form: A single integer (bytes).
questions.why_it_matters: Forces combining the dir-bounds inequality (dir_offset + dir_length <= F - 64), the 64-byte trailer-alignment rule, and the independent 128-byte whole-file floor for one specific (dir_offset, dir_length) pair, rather than reading any one rule's number off the page.

questions.question: A layer uses index_encoding 1 and has entry_count = 70,000. What is the exact byte length of its tile-index region (entry array plus segment-CRC array)? Answer as an integer number of bytes.
questions.answer_form: A single integer (bytes).
questions.why_it_matters: Applies the region-size formula (entry_count * 20 + ceil(entry_count / 2^16) * 4) to a count that is not an exact multiple of the segment size, requiring an actual ceiling-division computation rather than a table lookup.

questions.question: A planar layer declares codec 4 (lz4). Its tile extents give P = 2,000,000 sample positions per tile. It has two channels: channel a, type uint64, and channel b, type uint8. Is this layer's codec-4 declaration conforming? State the exact decoded byte size of whichever channel's plane governs the lz4 size check, and say which channel that is.
questions.answer_form: A verdict (conforming/not conforming), the governing channel's name, and its decoded size as an integer (bytes).
questions.why_it_matters: A bare recital of the lz4 cap is a table-quote; this requires computing each channel's own plane decoded size via its element size, identifying which one governs in a planar layer, and comparing that to the cap.

questions.question: A layer record declares per-tile alignment A = 4096 and slab run length S = 8, both nonzero, in the same layer record. Name the exact outcome class this produces and the register row (an "Lxx" label) it violates.
questions.answer_form: An outcome-class name and a register row label (e.g. "reject-layer, L20").
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the mutual-exclusivity carve-out between per-tile alignment and slab declarations, a prose rule rather than a table entry.

questions.question: A layer has dimension extents (7, 7) and tile extents (4, 4), with one int16 channel whose fill value is 0x2A2B. For the tile at tile coordinates (1, 1): how many of its sample positions are padding positions, and what two bytes, in storage order, does each padding position's channel value encode?
questions.answer_form: An integer count of padding positions, plus two hex bytes in storage order (e.g. "7 positions; bytes 2B 2A").
questions.why_it_matters: Combines grid/padding arithmetic for a non-exact tile fit with the rule that padding content is fixed to the channel's fill, encoded little-endian - a multi-step computation rather than a quoted example.

questions.question: A top-level user-metadata record (type 0x0002) is stored with flags MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1, PRESERVE_ON_EDIT = 0. Name the exact file-scope register row ("Fxx") that this stored-flag combination violates.
questions.answer_form: A single register row label (e.g. "F28").
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the exception that a registered type's fixed flags govern regardless of what bits are actually stored, and routes the mismatch to its own register row distinct from the general MU=1/PE=0 rule.

questions.question: A planar layer is read for channels r, g, b at one spatial position in a single request. Channel r's tile fails its stored-bytes CRC; channel g's tile is a valid sentinel; channel b's tile decodes cleanly. Must the reader fail the whole request, or may it return g's and b's values while reporting r's failure separately? Name the outcome class that governs r's failure.
questions.answer_form: A verdict ("may return g and b while reporting r separately" or "must fail the whole request") plus an outcome-class name.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the quantifier distinguishing a tile-scope failure, which is bounded per entry, from a layer-scope failure, which is not - the MAY/MUST NOT language of the tile-read algorithm's final step.

questions.question: True or false: an appender that extends a planar layer's channel list by one channel at the end (the layer having stored tiles in the generation the commit supersedes) may satisfy its re-emission obligation by appending only the new channel's tile-index entries, leaving the existing entries' bytes and position untouched.
questions.answer_form: True or false.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the exception that any change to a layer's stored-tile set or index content re-emits the whole tile-index region at a new placement, even where most entries are carried forward byte-identically - a rewording that drops the word "whole" changes the answer.

questions.question: A channel entry declares type uint32 and a fill field with length prefix 3. Name the exact register row ("Lxx") this violates.
questions.answer_form: A single register row label (e.g. "L30").
questions.why_it_matters: Requires looking up uint32's element size and comparing it against a concrete mismatched length prefix to land on a specific row, rather than reading a size off the type table directly.

questions.question: A layer's tile index has entry_count = 131,072, and every entry is the sentinel. How many segments does the index have, and what CRC-32C value (hex, upper-case) does the segment-CRC array hold for each of them?
questions.answer_form: An integer segment count plus one hex CRC value, upper-case, applying to every segment (e.g. "2 segments; 0xEECB3BB2 each").
questions.why_it_matters: 131,072 is an exact multiple of the segment size, so the final segment is also full rather than partial - testing the quantifier "for any full segment, final or not" against a case designed to tempt a wrong assumption that the last segment is always partial.

questions.question: A file's trailer has version_major = 1, version_minor = 5, no incompat-lane bits set, and ignore-lane bit 20 set. A reader implements only through version_minor 2 of major 1. Is the file accepted by this reader? Answer yes or no, and name any file-scope register row that would otherwise apply, or state that none does.
questions.answer_form: Yes/no plus a register-row label or "none".
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the quantifier "a reader MUST NOT reject a file for its version_minor" together with the defined non-violation for ignore-lane bits, against a scenario combining both at once so a reader cannot satisfy only one of them.

questions.question: A rewriter's input has a layer whose tile index contains an entry that §15.3 classifies reject-tile on a structural ground (not a stored-bytes CRC failure). Name the rewriter's two possible courses of action with respect to that layer.
questions.answer_form: An unordered list of exactly two named actions (e.g. "drop the layer; refuse to rewrite").
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the exception carved out when regenerating a relocated index region meets an entry with no stored extent to re-point - the rewriter can neither reproduce nor invent a replacement, leaving exactly two licensed disposals.

questions.question: A remote reader's transport does not disclose a range response's complete length, so the reader must probe the file size separately. What is the minimum number of round-trip requests this reader needs to complete the open (trailer validation plus directory fetch)? Answer as an integer.
questions.answer_form: A single integer.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the exception to the stated two-request baseline: the baseline already assumes the suffix-range response discloses the file size, so a transport that does not disclose it costs a third request - a quantifier easy to miss if one only remembers "two requests."

questions.question: A layer record declares rank 2, dimension extents (1000, 2000), tile extents (300, 500), layout = interleaved, and entry_count = 21. Name the exact register row ("Lxx") this layer violates.
questions.answer_form: A single register row label (e.g. "L21").
questions.why_it_matters: Requires computing the geometry-derived addressed-tile count from ceiling-division grid arithmetic on non-exact extents/tile-extents and comparing it against a declared entry_count, landing on one of several closely related index-mismatch rows.

questions.question: Partway through servicing a multi-tile request against one layer, step 3 of the tile-read algorithm detects an index-chain failure (a crc_of_crc_array or segment-CRC mismatch). (a) Name the outcome class and scope this failure takes. (b) May the reader still service the request's remaining tile entries from that same layer afterward? Answer yes or no.
questions.answer_form: An outcome-class/scope name plus a yes/no answer.
questions.why_it_matters: Tests the explicit contrast the document draws between a tile-scope failure (bounded to that entry) and a layer-scope index-chain failure detected at tile-use time, which instead bars the rest of the request and all further service from that layer.

answers.citations: tarn.md §7.4 (layer record table: entry_count equals the addressed-tile count [R-CNT-17]; extent_length formula under index_encoding 1); §11.3/§21.3 L21 (N = ∏⌈Eᵢ/Tᵢ⌉, planar addressed-tile count C·N)
answers.decisive_quote: entry_count | u64 | equals the addressed-tile count (§11.2, [R-CNT-17]) ... Under index_encoding 1, extent_length MUST equal entry_count × 20 + ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4

answers.citations: tarn.md §9.2 [R-LIF-02] and its second Note; worked minimal-file example (committed_file_length = 128 = the file size)
answers.decisive_quote: The new F is therefore at least the prior F plus 68, and since [R-CNT-06] makes every committed file length a multiple of 64, at least the prior F plus 128.
answers.reasoning: Smallest first commit is 128 bytes (shown directly in the spec's worked example). The spec's own Note derives that any commit's F is at least the prior F plus 128, generally (not only from offset 0). So smallest second commit F = 128 + 128 = 256.

answers.decisive_quote: Uniqueness is decided first, and over the raw name bytes whether or not each name is itself well-formed ... so two layers whose name fields are byte-identical are a duplicate even when neither name is valid.
answers.reasoning: The question's premise (each name field entirely within its record's inline_length) is exactly the condition under which a name field contributes to the namespace per §19.1. Name comparison is raw-byte comparison regardless of UTF-8 validity, so byte-identical ill-formed names are still a duplicate, which is a file-scope (reject-file) violation per [R-ENC-15].

answers.decisive_quote: whose response also carries the transport-authoritative file size F where the transport discloses a range response's complete length ([R-CNT-10], which governs where it does not: a reader that probes separately spends a third request, and one that cannot fails the open)
answers.reasoning: Baseline open is 2 requests (trailer suffix fetch + directory fetch). Since the transport never discloses the complete resource length, request 1 cannot supply the transport-authoritative F, and the reader isn't using suffix-window containment, so it must issue a separate size probe, for 3 total.

answers.decisive_quote: index-chain failures take layer scope ([R-IDX-04]) although their detection point is tile use ... The outcome is prospective: it bars further service from the layer, and does not retroactively invalidate content already returned under §19.2's validation timing ([R-RDR-02]).
answers.reasoning: A segment CRC / crc_of_crc_array mismatch is the index-chain failure the spec explicitly assigns to layer scope (reject-layer), not tile scope, and reject-layer is defined as prospective only — prior returned values are not retroactively invalidated.

answers.decisive_quote: A commit MAY make several of these changes at once, an extension and a shortening of one channel list excepted ... its name ... MAY change; a dimension extent MAY grow, and MUST NOT shrink; a planar layer's channel list MAY be extended at its end or shortened from its end, but not both in one commit
answers.reasoning: Rename, extent growth, and a channel-list shortening (not combined with an extension of the same list) are each individually permitted and the spec expressly allows combining several permitted changes in one commit; the question also stipulates every resulting declaration satisfies its bounds, matching the spec's further proviso.

answers.citations: tarn.md §21.2 row F36; §21.6 table (experimental/reserved MU=0 row)
answers.decisive_quote: A top-level record carries a type value from the reserved range 0x0003-0x7FFF, which this specification has not assigned; emitting one is a violation whatever its MU bit | — | verifier | certification ... a reserved-range type is read the same way [as an experimental-range MU=0 record], but emitting one is a violation (F36, L25)
answers.reasoning: Emitting a reserved-range type is always a conformance violation (F36), with the verifier as detector regardless of the MU bit; but the reader's processing (ignore-record at MU=0) is identical to how it handles an ordinary unassigned record at MU=0.

findings.title: No outcome class is stated for a reader lacking an assigned core codec/filter it is obliged to implement
findings.detail: R-CNF-03 declares software that cannot execute an assigned core codec/filter (e.g. zstd) non-conforming, but the document never states what such software's behavior is. §17.4's reject-layer treatment is grammatically confined to a conforming reader meeting a reserved/experimental codec value, not an assigned one it simply hasn't implemented. §21.9/R-ERR-04's resource-decline mechanism is scoped to the limits table's named quantities (rank, channels, entry_count, layers, dir_length, tile size, metadata size, zstd window) and never mentions codec/filter capability. §21.6's closing paragraph names exactly two 'conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses' (unimplemented format major; experimental-range top-level MU=1 type) and does not include this case. An implementer shipping a reader without zstd support gets no guidance on whether to refuse the whole file, reject only the layer, or serve the layer's declarations while refusing only its tile reads — all three are equally consistent with the text, since none of the three is a 'conforming reader' to begin with and no further constraint distinguishes them.
findings.quotation_a: "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Two implementations built from this text alone, each omitting zstd, can diverge on which bytes they will emit/accept from a file whose only defect (from their point of view) is a zstd-coded layer: one refuses the whole file (no bytes served from any layer), another serves every other layer and refuses only the zstd layer's tile reads, a third serves even that layer's name/geometry/channel declarations while refusing only sample data. All three satisfy every sentence the document states, so resolving the gap would change which of these three behaviors is sanctioned.

findings.title: Probe R4's field names (extent_offset/extent_length) do not match the document's tile-index-entry field names (offset/length)
findings.detail: This is not a defect in edition A; it is a note on the probe's own wording. The document's tile-index entry (§15.1) has fields named 'offset' and 'length'; 'extent_offset'/'extent_length' is the document's name for a different structure at a different scope — a record's extent slot (§7.2), which is never tested against the all-ones sentinel anywhere in the text. Read charitably as referring to the entry's offset/length fields, the condition in probe R4 maps cleanly onto register row T7. Flagged for transparency since a comparison across implementers answering the same probe from different texts could otherwise be thrown off by this naming mismatch, not because edition A itself is unclear.
findings.quotation_a: "0 | 8 | u64 | offset | structural | see §15.3 | 8 | 8 | u64 | length | structural | see §15.3" (§15.1 entry layout table)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is a terminology note about the probe's phrasing, not a claim that two implementations built from edition A alone would diverge on any byte — the document itself is internally consistent and unambiguous once the correct field names are substituted.

findings.title: No outcome class or register row for software that cannot execute a core, assigned codec or filter
findings.detail: The document mandates that every conforming reader implement all four assigned codecs and both assigned filters (they are core, with 'no subset profiles'); R-CNF-03 and R-COD-11 state that software failing this is categorically 'not a conforming reader,' but neither they nor §21's register assign that software an outcome class or behavior when it meets a layer validly declaring one of those assigned, core values anyway. Contrast the fully specified, adjacent case: a reserved or experimental codec value is a plain value-set violation under R-COD-03, register row L43, pinned to reject-layer with the layer's name still listable and every other layer unaffected. Concretely: a layer validly declares codec = 3 (zstd, assigned and core per §10.2). Implementation A, lacking a zstd decoder, treats this as reject-layer and serves the file's other layers; Implementation B treats it as reject-file and refuses the whole file; Implementation C returns zero-filled or garbage bytes for the layer's tiles. All three are equally consistent with R-CNF-03/R-COD-11's silence, which states only that the software itself falls outside the conformance classes — it supplies no bytes-level test by which one choice is correct and the others are not, because by its own framing the software making the choice has already left the set of actors the conformance classes govern. A second implementer answering this round's R3 from a different edition therefore has no textual anchor to converge on beyond 'such software is nonconforming,' and the two implementers' answers for what that software actually does can diverge arbitrarily while both remain faithful readings.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST... handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core... There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.quotation_b: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving the ambiguity changes which bytes such software may serve for the affected layer (fill values from reject-layer treatment, nothing at all from reject-file treatment, or raw/garbage decoded bytes from a 'best effort' treatment) and whether it may continue to serve every other layer in the file; the document supplies no comparison, checksum, or value-set test that selects among these, since the actor facing the choice is defined to be outside the reader conformance classes entirely.

As a byte sequence, the file is not conforming (its own physical tail fails the trailer gates). The next appender does not append: it must run the deliberate recovery scan (§9.6), re-verify the recovered state as a whole file, and truncate to that recovered length before any further commit.

findings.location_a: §20.3 step 4 ('the fixed declarations' / 'what the line gives up' / 'no check any actor owes able to see it' passage); [R-CNF-02]
findings.title: A fill-value-only change on a layer with no edge padding leaves no file-conformance witness, though the act is barred as conduct
findings.detail: §20.3 step 4 bars an appender from changing a stored-tile layer's fill value (among other fixed declarations); [R-CNF-02] explicitly classifies this bar as a conduct rule rather than a file-conformance predicate, and §20.3 step 4 itself narrows the independent witnesses of such a change to a short named list of register rows (T2-T5, T14, T17, T21-T25) plus outright decode/framing failure -- all of which require the layer to have edge-tile padding (§11.3) or a codec/filter change to fire. A writer implementing only the structural checks this specification obliges would, for a layer whose extent is an exact multiple of its tile extent (no edge padding), see a resulting file pass every §21 check and be certified conforming by a verifier, even though the writer that produced it violated the bound conduct rule. An implementer relying on 'the file will be rejected if I get this wrong' would be surprised: for the common case of evenly-tiled layers, nothing rejects it.
findings.quotation_a: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself ... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out. ... but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7).
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It determines, for the common case of a layer with no edge padding, which bytes a conforming verifier is obliged to accept and certify: a file produced by an impermissible fill-only commit and a file produced by a permissible one (same resulting bytes) are both certifiable as conforming, since no listed check fires. This is not a disagreement between two passages of the document -- it is the document's own explicit, self-consistent statement of a byte-level consequence that an implementer building only from the 'MUST NOT' sentence in §20.3 step 4 could easily miss without also reading [R-CNF-02] and §21.7's enumeration.

probe_answers.answer: Not permitted as an in-place append; fill is fixed for as long as a layer stores a tile. Operations offered instead: a new layer (drop the old one and add a new layer under the same name and new fill), or a whole-file rewrite that re-declares the layer under a fresh file_id. Whether the file such a commit would leave is nonconforming is not fixed outright: the bar itself is writer conduct with no register row, so the file is nonconforming only if some independent, witnessed check fires — for a fill-only change, that is T4 (padding content), which fires only if some stored tile of that layer has a padding position; a layer with no padding positions at all can remain fully conforming despite the conduct violation.

Next appender: treats the file as torn and must not append directly; runs the deliberate recovery scan, finds and whole-file re-verifies the prior trailer, truncates (or overwrites-then-truncates) to that committed length, then performs an ordinary commit from there.

findings.title: A creator that decodes an input file and re-emits it drops ignore-lane bits an appender/rewriter would keep
findings.detail: An appender and a rewriter are both bound to copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of their input unchanged (§6.3's [R-CNT-08]; §20.3 step 6; §20.5's [R-WRT-06]-adjacent text). A plain creator owes its input nothing at all, even one whose only input is the fully-decoded content of an existing TARN file: §20.1 states 'As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read... it writes flags = 0,' and §6.3 independently requires flags = 0 of any writer creating a file under this text. The tier distinction is keyed only to whether the output extends the input file under the same file_id, never to whether the writer happened to read that input first. A tool that reads a TARN file, decodes everything it understands, and writes a logically equivalent new file (rather than appending, or rewriting under §20.5's fresh-file_id procedure) is a creator, and silently loses any feature signalled only by a later-minor ignore-lane bit, with no MUST to report the loss and no register row recording it.
findings.quotation_a: As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving which tier a decode-then-recreate tool occupies changes the literal trailer bytes it must emit at the flags field — zero versus carrying bit 20 forward — and the document resolves it unambiguously to zero, a real, citable, byte-level consequence even though it is not an indeterminacy in the text.

findings.title: A fill-only change to a stored layer's conformance outcome turns entirely on whether any of its stored tiles has a padding position
findings.detail: §20.3 bars a commit from changing a stored layer's fill value, but states the bar 'binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms.' Working the fill-only case through the document's own witness list, the only check that can possibly fire is T4 (padding content, [R-SER-05]), and T4 has nothing to examine unless some stored tile of that layer actually has a padding position (an edge tile under §11.3/[R-GEO-04]). A layer whose every dimension's extent is an exact multiple of its tile extent has no padding anywhere, so a conduct-violating fill-only edit to such a layer can leave a file no stated verifier check anywhere in the document distinguishes from a conforming one — the writer broke a MUST, yet the resulting bytes pass every rule the document states.
findings.quotation_a: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Whether a verifier may certify the resulting file turns exactly on a literal, checkable fact about the edited layer's stored bytes — whether any stored tile has a padding position — which is precisely the condition T4 examines; for a padding-free layer no stated check rejects the file despite the writer-conduct violation, a determinate but easily-missed byte-level outcome.

findings.title: §15.1's tile-index region layout is the document's one unlabeled blockquote, and is therefore fully normative despite looking like an aside
findings.detail: `[R-CNF-01]` makes a blockquote non-normative only when labeled Note, Example, or Rationale; an unlabeled one is normative. Scanning every blockquote in the document for its leading label, exactly one carries none: the §15.1 statement that the tile-index region is, contiguously, an entry array followed by a segment-CRC array, with no padding anywhere inside the region. Every other blockquote in the document is a Note, an Example, or a Rationale. This one clause is fully binding, and [R-CNT-17]'s extent_length formula and [R-IDX-01]'s per-entry offset rule (entry k at region byte 20·k) both silently presuppose exactly this ordering and the absence of internal padding. An implementer applying a surface heuristic of 'blockquote formatting means aside, skip it' instead of checking the label, which is exactly the mistake `[R-CNF-01]`'s own phrasing is written to prevent, would miss that this is the one place the region's internal byte ordering is actually stated.
findings.quotation_a: the tile-index region addressed by the layer record's extent slot is, contiguously: [ entry array: entry_count × 20 bytes ] [ segment CRC array: ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4 bytes ]
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: If this clause were mistakenly treated as illustrative, an implementation could accept a tile-index region with the segment-CRC array placed before the entry array or with padding inserted between them, producing disagreement with another implementation about where entry k's 20 bytes actually sit, even though every other stated rule (the per-entry offset formula, the extent_length cross-check) would still nominally apply; the document's own labeling convention is exactly what forecloses that divergence, which is why the missing label on an otherwise-normative passage is worth flagging.

probe_answers.decisive_quote: "an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU = 1 (§10.2, §10.3): [R-CNT-15] obliges the reader to reject, and [R-CNF-02] makes the file conforming all the same."

probe_answers.answer: Assumed pads: no alignment/slab declared, so writers pack tightly except the commit protocol's forced pre-trailer pad to the next 64-byte boundary (20, 20, and 36 bytes for generations 1, 2, 3 respectively). F1=4,480; F2=13,120; F3=14,528 bytes (all multiples of 64). Live-state byte total at generation 3: 12,816 bytes. Slack total: 1,712 bytes (cross-checked two ways).
probe_answers.citations: §20.3 step 4/R-WRT-04 (re-emission on index-content change); §20.3 step 4/R-WRT-05 (untouched layer keeps its extent slot); §7.4/R-CNT-17 (index-region size formula); §9.2/R-LIF-02 (commit steps, pre-trailer pad); §5.2/R-CNT-21 (slack definition, includes pre-trailer pad); §9.7/R-LIF-08 (live-state claimants).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Every layer whose stored-tile set or index content this commit changes has its tile-index region re-emitted in full... and every other entry byte-identical at its disk-ordinal position... A layer... the commit leaves untouched [keeps] its extent slot, pointing at the existing region."

probe_answers.answer: Verdict: cannot establish for that layer (and the verifier MUST NOT certify the file), provided no violation was established elsewhere; the verifier reports that layer's decoded-content obligations (padding/fill, bool-byte rules) as unchecked, naming the codec/filter and the capability ground — not as a corruption finding. Caveat the document itself draws: if the undecodable codec value is reserved/experimental, that is already a layer-scope violation (L43/L45) detectable without any decode, so verdict is nonconforming instead and the cannot-establish branch is never reached; if the value is one of the four assigned/core codecs, R-CNF-03 states that software lacking it "is not a conforming reader" at all, which is the tension reported as finding verifiera-01.
probe_answers.citations: §17.4 (R-COD-11) in full; §2.3 (R-CNF-11's cannot-establish list); §2.3 (R-CNF-03, no-subset-profiles); §17.2 (R-COD-03, L43) and §17.3 (R-COD-09, L45).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file... software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03)."

probe_answers.answer: No: certification walks only the current generation's live committed state and has no mechanism to compare it against a prior generation's declarations, and even where bytes of a prior generation happen to survive as slack, this specific condition is expressly carved out of the file-conformance predicate and the register entirely — it is a writer-conduct rule, not a condition a file can exhibit, so no verdict follows from it either way. The file may be, and typically is, fully conforming.
probe_answers.citations: §9.7's closing Note ("does not depend on reconstructing the file's history"); §9.3's third Note (no field counts commits); §20.3 step 4's own text ("no register row records the violation itself... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit"); §2.3/R-CNF-02 (names this exact case among its conduct-rule examples); §21.7/R-ERR-01 (the test for "no condition a file can exhibit").
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit."

probe_answers.answer: Two simultaneous effects at two actors. Every reader/updater treats the stored PE bit as 1 regardless of what is on disk ("never silently deletable") — a content-level reading, not a rejection. The verifier additionally treats the stored MU=1/PE=0 combination itself as a violation at the record's governing scope: file scope / reject-file for a non-layer top-level record (register row F25), or layer scope / reject-layer for a layer record or a layer sub-record (register row L46). Both rows are detector=verifier, detected at certification, not at open or layer access.
probe_answers.citations: §7.2 (R-CNT-12) in full; §21.2 row F25; §21.3 row L46; §2.4 (owning-scope mapping file/layer -> reject-file/reject-layer).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: "Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1... a verifier MUST treat... the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope."

findings.title: R-CNF-11's unqualified 'cannot execute a codec or filter' ground for cannot-establish is not reconciled with R-CNF-03's blanket, class-level disqualification
findings.detail: R-CNF-11 (§2.3) names, as a standing ground for the cannot-establish verdict, 'when it cannot execute a codec or filter (R-COD-11)' with no restriction to reserved/experimental values. Read alone, this licenses any verifier — including one missing a core codec such as zstd or lz4 — to report cannot-establish layer-by-layer while otherwise certifying files that do not use the missing codec, remaining a 'conforming verifier' throughout. But R-CNF-03 (§2.3) states, with no per-file qualifier, that 'software that declines to support a core codec... is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly,' and verifiers 'inherit every reader obligation' (§2.3). R-COD-11's own second sentence (§17.4) then narrows the only circumstance in which an actually-conforming reader can be in the 'cannot execute' position at all to a reserved or experimental codec/filter value, since every assigned one is core. The document never rewrites R-CNF-11's phrasing to reflect that narrowing, so an implementer reading R-CNF-11 in isolation is not told whether a verifier lacking a core codec may still legitimately certify other files under the conforming-verifier label (reading a) or is disqualified from that class for every file it processes (reading b).
findings.quotation_a: "There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly." (R-CNF-03) vs. "...when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11])..." (R-CNF-11, §2.3) vs. "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])." (R-COD-11, §17.4)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Under reading (a) a verifier missing a core codec may certify, as conforming, files that only use codecs it does support; under reading (b) that same software is disqualified from the conforming-verifier/conforming-reader class entirely, and none of its accept/reject outputs — for any file, including ones that never touch the missing codec — count as a conforming verifier's verdicts under this specification. That is a direct disagreement about which files an implementation may validly certify and under what label, not merely a difference in how a result is phrased.

probe_answers.answer: Three verdicts only: conforming, nonconforming, cannot establish. Conforming: no violation established anywhere and nothing left uncheckable. Nonconforming: at least one violation established anywhere, in any scope -- this verdict takes absolute priority over everything else, however many requirements were left unchecked. Cannot establish: some requirement was unable to be checked on a capability or resource ground (named grounds: unimplemented format major, unimplemented top-level MU=1 record type, an uncomputable codec or filter, a declined layer/tile decode on resource grounds, a declined user-metadata document decode) AND no violation was established elsewhere; a verifier reporting this verdict MUST NOT certify the file.
probe_answers.citations: [R-CNF-11] (§2.3) in full, including the sentence beginning 'An established violation takes priority'; the capability/resource-ground list restated at §21.6's 'A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground...' paragraph.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: An established violation takes priority: a verifier that has established any violation reports nonconforming, however many requirements it was unable to check, and cannot establish is available only to a traversal that established no violation.

probe_answers.answer: Reserved range (0x0003-0x7FFF) with MU=1: verdict is nonconforming, reject-file, recorded against the narrower register row F35 (an instance of the broader F36, per §21.1's specialization list), fixed by [R-CNT-15] (the MU-bit rule) combined with the independent rule that emitting any reserved-range value at all is itself a violation regardless of MU bit (F36). Experimental range (>=0x8000) with MU=1: the reader still rejects the file (same action, [R-CNT-15]), but [R-CNF-02] makes the file itself conforming all the same -- this is one of §21.6's two named 'conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses.' For a verifier specifically, this exact scenario is named in §21.6 as a cannot-establish ground, so the verdict is cannot establish (assuming no other violation exists), never nonconforming. The two cases are not in tension: the reserved case carries an independent MU-bit-indifferent violation (F36) the experimental case explicitly lacks.
probe_answers.citations: [R-CNT-15] (§7.2, restated §7.3, §10.3); register rows F35 and F36 (§21.2); §21.1's specialization-list sentence naming 'F35 of F36'; §21.6's two paragraphs ('Two structural cases are conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses... The second is an experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU = 1' and 'A verifier is unable to check a requirement... as when... a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement'); [R-CNF-02] (§2.3).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: the same type as a layer sub-record is reject-layer and never a ground to refuse the file (R-CNT-18), so only the top-level case is a file a reader refuses, since the prohibition on publishing experimental values binds a writer's conduct and not the bytes.

probe_answers.answer: Assumed pads: pad1=20 bytes, pad2=20 bytes, pad3=36 bytes (each the gap from the end of that generation's directory to the next 64-byte boundary; no alignment/slab declared so no other inter-structure gaps). F (final committed file length, generation 3) = 14,528 bytes. Live-state byte total = 12,816 bytes (front 16 + layer A's live tiles 4,096 + A's re-emitted index region 84 + layer B's untouched tiles 8,192 + B's untouched index region 164 + directory3 200 + trailer3 64). Slack total a completing coverage walk reports = 1,712 bytes (= F - live, cross-checked by independently enumerating five discrete slack regions: the superseded generation-1 A index region 84, generation-1's directory+pad+trailer superseded by gen 2 (284), the one superseded 1,024-byte A tile, generation-2's directory+pad+trailer superseded by gen 3 (284), and pad3 itself (36), totaling 1,712 exactly).
probe_answers.citations: [R-LIF-02] step 5 (pad to next 64-byte boundary); [R-WRT-04] (a layer whose stored-tile set changes has its whole tile-index region re-emitted in full, necessarily at a new placement, with every other entry byte-identical at its disk-ordinal position); [R-WRT-05] (an untouched layer's record and extent slot are carried forward byte-identically); §5.2/[R-CNT-21] (slack is everything the live state does not claim; a completing walk's total is exact).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Every layer whose stored-tile set or index content this commit changes has its tile-index region re-emitted in full, entry_count entries plus the segment CRC array, necessarily at a new placement...

probe_answers.answer: Verdict: cannot establish (provided the verifier established no violation elsewhere in the file) -- the verifier MUST NOT certify the file. The report on that layer: the verifier names the requirement it was unable to check and the ground (the specific codec/filter value and the layer it governs), per [R-CNF-11]'s per-requirement reporting duty; the layer is reported as unchecked, not as rejected and not as examined-clean. This scenario can only honestly arise for one of the four assigned (core) codecs or either assigned filter, since a reserved/experimental codec or filter value is instead the ordinary value-set violation L43/L45, not a 'cannot execute' capability case.
probe_answers.citations: [R-COD-11] (§17.4) in full; [R-CNF-11] (§2.3)'s per-requirement reporting duty; [R-CNF-03] (§2.3)'s 'no subset profiles' rule and §17.2's 'all four are core' statement, read together as the reason this scenario presupposes an assigned value.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file. That inability is not a finding that the file is nonconforming, and it fixes the file's verdict as cannot establish only where the verifier established no violation elsewhere.

probe_answers.answer: In general, no: the verifier's coverage walk is defined entirely over the live state reached from the live trailer, and the document is explicit that 'Nothing here enumerates prior commits... does not depend on reconstructing the file's history.' Changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile is a writer-conduct violation that §20.3 says makes 'no file... nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself,' and §21.7 names this class of thing explicitly as 'unwitnessed.' Exception: if the new declaration happens to break one of a handful of structurally-witnessed content checks for a tile carried forward unmodified (decoded-size exactness T3, padding/pad-bit fill T4/T5, boolean-byte validity T2, or a codec-framing check under a changed codec/filter T14/T17/T21/T22/T24/T25), the verifier WILL detect that symptom and report nonconforming at that row's own scope -- but it will never report it as 'a declaration changed across generations,' since no field records that fact at all. Absent such a symptom, the verifier certifies the file (if nothing else is wrong), seeing no byte-level evidence anything happened.
probe_answers.citations: §9.7 ('A verifier checking [R-CNT-02]'s partition walks the live state only' and its closing Note); §20.3's bar on changing fixed declarations and its own Note on why there is no register row; §21.7's definition of 'unwitnessed' and its parenthetical list of the symptomatic rows (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2, T17, T24, T25).
probe_answers.decisive_quote: under new [declarations] the same bytes would denote values, coordinates or padding the writer did not store, with every checksum in §8 certifying the result and, but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7).

probe_answers.answer: The verifier treats MU=1 with PE=0 as a validity error (file-conformance violation) at the record's own governing scope: file scope / reject-file (register row F25) if the record is a non-layer top-level record, or layer scope / reject-layer (register row L46) if it is a layer record or one of its sub-records. This is detector=verifier in both cases, detected at certification. An ordinary reader or updater (not acting as verifier) is NOT obliged to reject anything over this combination; it simply treats the stored PE bit as if it were 1 regardless of what is stored ('never silently deletable'), so the record is preserved and conforming read/update behavior is otherwise unaffected -- only the verifier's certification is blocked by it.
probe_answers.citations: [R-CNT-12] (§7.2) in full; register rows F25 (§21.2) and L46 (§21.3); Appendix H's conforming-verifier checklist restating 'MU = 1 with PE = 0... [R-CNT-12], [R-CNT-22]'.
probe_answers.decisive_quote: Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable)... a verifier MUST treat a nonzero reserved flag bit or the MU = 1 with PE = 0 combination as a validity error at the record's governing scope.

findings.title: Undetermined whether codec-incapable software is ever a 'conforming verifier' at all
findings.detail: R-CNF-03 states an absolute, exception-free bar: 'MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core... There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.' R-CNF-11 says a (conforming) verifier 'inherits every reader obligation,' which on its face includes this one unconditionally. Yet R-COD-11 and §21.6 both describe 'a verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter' as ordinary, licensed behavior that produces a defined report ('cannot establish'), using the very three-verdict vocabulary §2.3 reserves for the 'conforming verifier' class. An implementer building a verifier that is missing, say, an lz4 decoder must decide: (a) such software fails R-CNF-03's bar and is therefore not a conforming reader/verifier at all, so none of its output (for any file, not just lz4 ones) carries the normative weight of a certification; or (b) R-COD-11 implicitly carves out codec/filter execution as a capability ground on par with an unimplemented format major (whose non-support R-CNF-03 explicitly scopes as acceptable: 'every conforming file of a format major version it implements'), letting such software still issue valid cannot-establish verdicts for the affected layers while fully certifying others. The document never states which reading governs.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file. [...] For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03).
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementer built from reading (b) alone produces software that, on meeting an unsupported-but-assigned codec, issues a 'cannot establish' report for just that layer and proceeds to fully certify the rest of the file (accepting/rejecting other layers' bytes on their own merits). An implementer built from reading (a) alone produces software that, on the same file, refuses to issue any verdict at all (since it holds itself disqualified from the verifier class the moment it lacks a core codec), and a pipeline consuming its output would have to treat every one of its reports -- including ones about files using only codec 1 -- as having no standing. The two implementations therefore accept/report differently on the identical byte stream whenever a core codec is unavailable to them, which is exactly the byte-level test: does resolving the ambiguity change what a conforming implementation may emit, or must accept or reject? Here it changes what the tool is entitled to assert at all.

findings.title: Cross-generation declaration changes are explicitly, by design, invisible to the verifier's live-state walk
findings.detail: §20.3 bars a commit from changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile, but states plainly that this bar binds the commit only as a writer-conduct rule: 'no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself.' §9.7 and its closing Note confirm the verifier's coverage walk only ever reaches the live trailer/directory and never reconstructs history. §21.7 names this the 'unwitnessed' category and gives the specific, narrow list of symptomatic rows (T2, T3, T4, T5, T14, T17, T21, T22, T24, T25) through which such a change can incidentally surface -- but only as an ordinary tile-scope finding, never attributed to its true cause. This is not a flaw I am alleging (the document states it as deliberate design, repeatedly and explicitly), but it is a real limit on what a 'conforming verifier' certifies: certification never implies that a layer's current declarations are consistent with what any earlier generation stored under the same layer, only that the live state as given is internally sound.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, R-ERR-01, R-CNF-02)
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is a documented design limit, not an underdetermination: resolving it changes nothing about which bytes any conforming implementation may emit or must accept/reject, since the document is explicit and internally consistent about exactly this behavior; I report it as context an implementer should have, not as a gap needing a byte-level resolution.

result.summary: Both walks (reader-a from edition A, reader-b from edition B) answered probes R1-R8 correctly and identically in outcome class, register row, and scope. I confirmed by direct side-by-side reading that every governing section either walk cited (§2.3-2.4, §4.2, §5.1, §6.2-6.4, §9.7, §10.1-10.2, §11.4, §14.2, §15.1-15.3, §17.2, §17.4, §19.1, §21.2, §21.4, §21.6) states the same rules, quantifiers and worked arithmetic in both editions. §21.2's and §21.4's markdown register tables (rows F1-F36, T1-T26) are byte-identical between editions. Edition B is a faithful readability rewrite of A for every section I checked: sentences are shortened, dashes and appositives split out, and a handful of explanatory asides are trimmed or relocated, but I found no case where the two editions decide a probe differently, so none of R1-R8 carries a LOSS or ADDITION. R3 (the zstd / assigned-but-unimplemented-codec case) is the one probe where both walks independently flagged the document itself as underdetermined; I verified the underlying passages (§2.3 R-CNF-03, §17.2 R-COD-03, §17.4 R-COD-11, §21.6's closing paragraph, §21.9 R-ERR-04) are substantively identical in both editions, so this is an AMBIGUITY carried over unrepaired by the rewrite, not a divergence between A and B. Reading past the probes per the charter, I found three places where A states an explanatory clause that B's corresponding section omits: (1) §2.3's conforming-reader bullet drops A's aside that an unimplemented MU=1 top-level type in a conforming file is "necessarily from the experimental range" — still fully derivable from §21.6's and register row F36's unchanged text, so EQUIVALENT; (2) §2.3's conforming-verifier bullet's inline list of "cannot establish" grounds is relocated verbatim-in-substance to a new closing paragraph of B's §21.6, with §2.3 now pointing there — a reorganization, not a loss; (3) §2.4 drops a sentence pair stating that "ignore-record" vocabulary also covers non-violations and that preserve-verbatim is "orthogonal to reader outcomes" — the preserve-verbatim table row and the usage pattern itself survive unchanged in B, so no requirement or byte-level behavior is affected, though this is the one trim with no verbatim restatement elsewhere and is worth a maintainer's attention as a readability regression. None of these three changes the outcome, register row, or any byte that an implementation built from one edition alone would produce differently from one built from the other. I found no REPORTER_ERROR (no walker answered incorrectly from a text that decided the question), no CONTRADICTION, and no case where one edition forced a guess the other's walker avoided — both walks' own citation sets draw from the same substantive passages in both editions. readera-02's observation about probe R4's field-naming (extent_offset/extent_length vs. the document's own offset/length) is a probe-wording artifact common to both editions, not a textual divergence.

findings.title: Both editions equally fail to assign an outcome to a reader lacking a core, assigned codec/filter (R3)
findings.detail: Both walks independently found that neither edition assigns a register row, outcome class, or behavioral obligation to software that is categorically "not a conforming reader" because it cannot execute an assigned core codec (e.g. zstd, codec 3) that a layer validly declares, as distinct from the fully specified reserved/experimental-value case (reject-layer, row L43, [R-COD-03]). I read §2.3, §17.2, §17.4, §21.6 and §21.9 in both editions and confirmed the controlling sentences are substantively identical word for word, including [R-COD-11]'s sentence confining reject-layer to "a reserved or experimental value." This is not a rewrite-introduced or rewrite-fixed divergence; the gap is carried over unchanged. An implementation built from A alone and one built from B alone are equally underdetermined and can equally diverge from a third implementation of the same edition, but not from each other in a way the text decides.
findings.quotation_a: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]).
findings.quotation_b: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: The indeterminacy is edition-invariant: neither text decides the question, so there is no edition-attributable byte or verdict difference — any divergence among implementations would occur independently under either edition alone, not because one edition says something the other doesn't.

result.summary:
Both writer-implementer walks (transcript-writer-a.md on edition A, transcript-writer-b.md on edition B) reach identical answers to all eleven probes (W1–W11), and I verified this is not coincidental agreement on divergent texts: I re-read every section either walker cited — §2.3, §4.5, §5.1, §6.1–6.4, §7.1–7.3, §9.2, §9.4–9.6, §11.3, §15.1, §15.4, §20.1, §20.3 (full, both worked examples and all three commit-shape figures), §20.4 (full, including the three-row preservation table), §20.5 (full), §21.1, §21.4 (the full T1–T26 tile-scope register table), §21.6, §21.7, Appendix A (full byte table), and Appendix G (all 12 items) — directly in both editions, side by side. Every one of these sections is either byte-for-byte identical (confirmed by diff for §20.3, §20.4/§20.5, Appendix A, Appendix G, the §21.4 register table) or substance-for-substance identical with only sentence-boundary, list-vs-prose, or punctuation differences. No rule, exception, quantifier, worked figure, table row, byte value, or requirement-ID citation differs between editions anywhere I checked, so none of W1–W11 shows a LOSS, ADDITION, or REPORTER_ERROR — all are EQUIVALENT at the byte level: an implementation built from either edition alone would emit the same bytes and reach the same accept/reject verdicts for every probed scenario.

I found three places where content is genuinely relocated rather than merely reworded (the rewriter's ignore-lane-copy-forward rule, stated in both §6.3 and §20.5 in A but only in §20.5 in B; the verifier's "cannot establish" grounds, spelled out in §2.3 in A but abbreviated there and restated in full in §21.6 in B; and the user-metadata quarantine paragraph, in §7.1 in A but moved to §7.3 in B) — each confirmed to preserve the content in full, so each is EQUIVALENT (reorganization, not loss).

I also checked each walk's own numbered findings against the other edition, per the charter's instruction to ask whether a defect one walk flagged is edition-specific. All three of edition B's findings (writerb-01, -02, -03) and edition A's one finding (writera-01) rest on passages I confirmed are identical in edition A, so none is actually B-specific (or A-specific): writera-01 and writerb-02 are the same fact independently found from identical text; writerb-01's creator/updater asymmetry is equally derivable from A's identical §20.1; and writerb-03's claim that §15.1 holds the document's one unlabeled, hence normative, blockquote is equally true of A, which carries the identical unlabeled blockquote in the identical position. None of these is a fidelity divergence between editions — each is a correct observation about a feature of the one format both editions describe equally.

Neither transcript shows a forced guess, a re-read, or a hedge on any probe; walker A read a narrower explicit section list than walker B's full front-to-back pass, but every citation either walker used resolves inside sections A did read, so the narrower reading cost nothing on this charter. I found no AMBIGUITY, no CONTRADICTION, and no case where the two walkers agreed on an answer "by luck" against actually-differing texts.

F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine... F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.

result.summary: The single divergence for slate B, quizb-quizb-q3, is EQUIVALENT: both takers gave the same verdict (conforming), named the same governing channel (a, uint64), and gave the same decoded size (16,000,000 bytes), and every passage either edition's text turns on is byte-identical in substance between A and B. §12.1's type table gives uint64 element size 8 and uint8 element size 1 in both editions, word-for-word. §14.2's decoded-size formula for a planar numeric channel, P·Bᶜ, is stated identically in both editions (only connective punctuation differs: A joins two clauses with an em dash where B uses a colon, and A's "a planar bool plane is sized by packing" sentence differs from B's only in a comma vs. em-dash joiner — no formula or table content changes). §17.2's codec-4 clause, tagged [R-COD-07], states the same 0x7E000000 decoded-size cap and the same "in a planar layer each channel's plane carries its own decoded size ... and the largest governs" rule in both editions, differing only in whether that final clause is set off by an em dash (A) or begins a new sentence (B). §21.3's table row L44, which both editions carry at the identical row id with identical condition text ("Codec 4 (lz4) declared on a layer any of whose addressed tiles' decoded size exceeds 0x7E000000 bytes — in a planar layer the largest channel plane governs"), is byte-for-byte identical between the two files (A line 3938, B line 3730). Both takers' arithmetic checks out independently: 2,000,000 × 8 = 16,000,000 (channel a, uint64) versus 2,000,000 × 1 = 2,000,000 (channel b, uint8); channel a is larger and governs; 0x7E000000 = 2,113,929,216, and 16,000,000 is well under that cap, so the declaration is conforming in both editions under identical rules. I found no LOSS, ADDITION, or REPORTER_ERROR here: neither taker misread anything, and the two editions decide the question identically — the surface differences between their citation styles (taker A cited "§17.2 R-COD-07/L44"; taker B additionally cited row L2 and spec/tarn.md's exact section path) reflect only which of several, textually-equivalent anchors to the same rule each taker chose to name, not any difference in what the rule says. This is a case where the mechanical matcher's flag is explained entirely by phrasing/citation-style variance between the takers, not by any edition-level divergence.

quizDivergences.title: Slate B quizb-q3: the editions' takers answer differently
quizDivergences.detail:
QUESTION: A planar layer declares codec 4 (lz4). Its tile extents give P = 2,000,000 sample positions per tile. It has two channels: channel a, type uint64, and channel b, type uint8. Is this layer's codec-4 declaration conforming? State the exact decoded byte size of whichever channel's plane governs the lz4 size check, and say which channel that is.
FROM A: conforming; channel a; 16000000 [high] cites §14.2 (planar numeric decoded size = P·Bᶜ); §12.1 (element sizes uint64=8, uint8=1); §17.2 R-COD-07/L44 (largest channel plane governs the lz4 cap of 0x7E000000)
FROM B: conforming; a; 16000000 [high] cites spec/tarn.md §17.2 codec-4 clause [R-COD-07]; §21.3 rows L2/L44; §12 type table (uint8=1 byte, uint64=8 bytes)
A's reasoning: Channel a (uint64): 2,000,000×8=16,000,000; channel b (uint8): 2,000,000×1=2,000,000. a is larger and governs; 16,000,000 < 0x7E000000 (2,113,929,216), so the declaration is conforming.
B's reasoning: Channel a (uint64): 2,000,000×8=16,000,000 bytes; channel b (uint8): 2,000,000 bytes. 16,000,000 is larger, governs, and is well under the 0x7E000000 (2,113,929,216) cap, so conforming.

quizDivergences.quotation_b: Writers MUST NOT declare this codec for a layer any of whose addressed tiles' decoded size exceeds 0x7E000000 bytes ... In a planar layer each channel's plane carries its own decoded size ... and the largest governs.

findings.title: Both editions equally fail to assign an outcome to a reader lacking a core, assigned codec/filter (R3)
findings.detail: Both walks independently found that neither edition assigns a register row, outcome class, or behavioral obligation to software that is categorically "not a conforming reader" because it cannot execute an assigned core codec (e.g. zstd, codec 3) that a layer validly declares, as distinct from the fully specified reserved/experimental-value case (reject-layer, row L43, [R-COD-03]). I read §2.3, §17.2, §17.4, §21.6 and §21.9 in both editions and confirmed the controlling sentences are substantively identical word for word, including [R-COD-11]'s sentence confining reject-layer to "a reserved or experimental value." This is not a rewrite-introduced or rewrite-fixed divergence; the gap is carried over unchanged. An implementation built from A alone and one built from B alone are equally underdetermined and can equally diverge from a third implementation of the same edition, but not from each other in a way the text decides.
findings.quotation_a: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]).
findings.quotation_b: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: The indeterminacy is edition-invariant: neither text decides the question, so there is no edition-attributable byte or verdict difference — any divergence among implementations would occur independently under either edition alone, not because one edition says something the other doesn't.

The dropped text is an explanatory inference, not an independent rule, and no requirement ID attaches to it.
