findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports cannot establish ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: The content moved, it did not disappear: every ground and citation is present in both editions, so no implementer's behavior differs.

findings.title: B drops A's sentences on ignore-record vocabulary covering non-violations and preserve-verbatim's orthogonality
findings.detail: A's §2.4 follows the outcome-class sentence with two further sentences: that the same vocabulary applies to non-violations (an unknown ancillary record is "ignored," not rejected) and that preserve-verbatim is an updater obligation orthogonal to reader outcomes, so a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves. B omits both sentences and goes straight to the outcome table. Of the three trims found in this round, this is the only one with no verbatim restatement elsewhere in B. However the preserve-verbatim table row itself, and its operative definition, are unchanged in B's table immediately following, and the usage pattern the first dropped sentence names (ignore-record applied to a non-violation) is still demonstrated by example in both editions' §21.6 table (e.g. the experimental-range metadata-encoding row says "Ignored (ignore-record)"). No requirement ID attaches to either dropped sentence.
findings.quotation_a: The same vocabulary is used for defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is ignored, not rejected). preserve-verbatim names an updater obligation, orthogonal to reader outcomes: a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: No requirement ID attaches to either dropped sentence, and the operative preserve-verbatim rule (the table row, and §20.4's own treatment) is unchanged in B, so no byte or verdict a conforming implementation produces differs; flagged as a readability regression worth a maintainer's attention since, unlike the other two trims, it has no verbatim counterpart anywhere else in B.

findings.title: writera-01 and writerb-02 are the same finding, independently derived from identical text in both editions
findings.detail: Walker A's writera-01 and walker B's writerb-02 both observe that a fill-value-only change on a layer with no edge padding leaves no §21 witness even though it violates §20.3 step 4's conduct bar. I confirmed §20.3 step 4, the §21.4 T4 register row, and §11.3's edge-padding rule are identical (the T4 row is byte-for-byte identical by diff) in both editions. This is not a divergence between A and B; it is one true fact about the one format, correctly found twice from the same source text.
findings.quotation_a: A change to any fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile in the generation the commit supersedes — a fill value, a type, a tile extent — is not an appender's operation at all (step 4): it would reinterpret or invalidate every stored tile it reaches.
findings.quotation_b: A change to any fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile in the generation the commit supersedes (a fill value, a type, a tile extent) is not an appender's operation at all (step 4): it would reinterpret or invalidate every stored tile it reaches.
findings.byte_level_rationale: No implementation divergence: both editions state the identical rule and the identical T4 witness chain, so a writer built from either alone behaves identically on this scenario.

findings.location_a: §20.1 ('As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input...')
findings.title: writerb-01's creator/updater ignore-lane asymmetry is equally derivable from edition A's identical §20.1 text
findings.detail: Walker B's writerb-01 finding (a creator that decodes-and-re-emits an existing file loses ignore-lane bits an appender/rewriter would keep) rests on §20.1's creator/rewriter distinction, which I confirmed is word-for-word identical in both editions. Walker A's own W5 answer reaches the identical conclusion from the identical sentence, though A did not promote it to a numbered finding. Not a B-specific defect or addition.
findings.quotation_a: As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0, and it answers for every byte of its output (`[R-CNF-05]`), bytes it copied from another file included.
findings.quotation_b: As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0, and it answers for every byte of its output (`[R-CNF-05]`), bytes it copied from another file included.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Identical text in both editions; no implementer reading A alone would miss this rule any more than one reading B alone.

findings.title: writerb-03's 'one unlabeled blockquote' observation about §15.1 is equally true of edition A
findings.detail: Walker B's writerb-03 flags §15.1's tile-index region-layout line as the document's one unlabeled (hence, under `[R-CNF-01]`, fully normative) blockquote, easy to miss as an aside. Direct extraction shows edition A's §15.1 carries the identical unlabeled blockquote in the identical position, followed by the identical 'with no padding anywhere inside the region' sentence. The risk writerb-03 names is exactly as present in A as in B; this is a true fact about the shared format, not a B-specific editorial quirk.
findings.quotation_a: [ entry array: entry_count × 20 bytes ] [ segment CRC array: ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4 bytes ]\n\nwith no padding anywhere inside the region.
findings.quotation_b: [ entry array: entry_count × 20 bytes ] [ segment CRC array: ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4 bytes ]\n\nwith no padding anywhere inside the region.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Identical blockquote, identically unlabeled, in both editions; an implementer's risk of treating it as an aside is the same reading either edition.

findings.title: The rewriter's ignore-lane-copy-forward rule is stated twice in edition A (§6.3 and §20.5) but only once in edition B (§20.5 alone)
findings.detail: Edition A's §6.3 adds 'A rewriter, though its output is a new file, carries the input's unknown ignore-lane bits into its output trailer rather than writing flags = 0, and sets no other (§20.5, [R-WRT-06])' immediately before the general updater sentence; edition B's §6.3 omits this restatement and states the rule only in §20.5, where both editions carry it verbatim-identically. A pure consolidation: content fully preserved, said once instead of twice.
findings.quotation_a: A rewriter, though its output is a new file, carries the input's unknown ignore-lane bits into its output trailer rather than writing flags = 0, and sets no other (§20.5, `[R-WRT-06]`).
findings.quotation_b: absent (§6.3 moves directly from the flag-lane paragraph to 'An updater MUST copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits...' with no separate rewriter sentence; the same rule appears only in §20.5, identically in both editions)
findings.byte_level_rationale: W5's answer in both transcripts already cites §20.5 (not §6.3) for this rule, and §20.5's text is identical, so no probe answer or implementer behavior differs.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conforming verifier bullet (full 'cannot establish' grounds list)
findings.location_b: §2.3 (abbreviated to '(§21.6 names the grounds)') and §21.6 (new closing paragraph restating the list)
findings.title: The verifier's 'cannot establish' grounds list is relocated from §2.3 (A) to a new §21.6 closing paragraph (B), not dropped or changed
findings.detail: Edition A spells out all five 'cannot establish' grounds inline in §2.3. Edition B's §2.3 cross-references '(§21.6 names the grounds)' and B's §21.6 carries a closing paragraph not present in A's §21.6, restating the identical five grounds. Confirmed by direct extraction of both §2.3 and §21.6 in both editions.
findings.quotation_a: as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter (`[R-COD-11]`), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations (`[R-ERR-04]`, `[R-SER-05]`, `[R-SER-08]`), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document (`[R-MTA-09]`)
findings.quotation_b: A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* (`[R-CNF-11]`), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter (`[R-COD-11]`, §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations (`[R-ERR-04]`, `[R-SER-05]`, `[R-SER-08]`), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document (`[R-MTA-09]`)
findings.byte_level_rationale: Same five grounds, same requirement-ID citations, only moved between sections; no requirement's content changes.

findings.title: The user-metadata quarantine paragraph is relocated from §7.1 (A) to §7.3 (B), not dropped
findings.detail: Edition A's §7.1 carries the full 'Metadata compression exists only at record granularity... User metadata is quarantined...' paragraph. Edition B's §7.1 is a two-sentence stub about the directory region's own CRC, and the quarantine paragraph (reworded, same obligations: extent-slot validity, encoding values, ignore-record/SHOULD-report, the [R-CNF-08] override, the resource-decline carve-out) reappears as the second half of B's §7.3, right after the registry flag table. Confirmed by direct extraction of A §7.1 and B §7.1+§7.3.
findings.quotation_a: Metadata compression exists only at record granularity. Each user-metadata record carries its document in its extent — never inline — and declares the document's encoding in its own inline payload... User metadata is quarantined: each way a user-metadata record's document can be unreadable once its framing has been read... is ignore-record with a SHOULD-report, notwithstanding the owning-scope mapping of `[R-CNF-08]`.
findings.quotation_b: Each user-metadata record carries its document in its extent, never inline, and declares the document's encoding in its own inline payload... User metadata is quarantined. Once a user-metadata record's framing has been read, each way its document can be unreadable is ignore-record with a SHOULD-report... The quarantine overrides the owning-scope mapping of `[R-CNF-08]`.
findings.byte_level_rationale: All obligations (quarantine scope, SHOULD-report, [R-CNF-08] override, resource-decline carve-out) are present in both editions' text; only the section housing them differs.

findings.title: Verifier-a's V2 answer treats F35 and F36 as both firing; both editions' §21.1 says record against the narrower row (F35) alone
findings.detail: Verifier-a's probe-V2 answer states that for a reserved-range top-level record carrying MU=1, both register rows F35 (MU=1 specifically) and F36 (reserved-range emission alone) 'fire' as if independently applicable. Verifier-b's V2 answer instead invokes §21.1's specialization rule and says the file is 'recorded against the narrower row F35' alone, F36 not separately recorded. I read §21.1's specialization-list sentence in both editions and it is byte-identical in substance: '...F35 of F36, L24 of L25, F21 of F22 and L10 of L11 stand in that relation... the file is recorded against the narrower row, whose detector and detection point are the ones that apply.' Edition A's own text therefore states the same narrowing rule verifier-b used from edition B, and verifier-a's own transcript elsewhere (its charter write-up, item 5 of 'Every register row's detector and outcome') correctly lists 'F35 within F36' as one of the specialization pairs — so verifier-a's V2 answer contradicts a rule verifier-a itself correctly identified from the very same (A) text. An implementer who built strictly from either edition's §21.1 sentence would attribute the file solely to F35, not to both F35 and F36 — matching verifier-b's answer, not verifier-a's, in both editions equally.
findings.quotation_a: Some rows are strict specializations of others: where every file exhibiting one row's condition... necessarily exhibits another's, the file is recorded against the narrower row, whose detector and detection point are the ones that apply. F1's front-block instance of F6 and its trailer-magic instance of F8, F35 of F36, L24 of L25, F21 of F22 and L10 of L11 stand in that relation; the property decides any pair and this list is not offered as closed.
findings.quotation_b: Some rows are strict specializations of others: where every file exhibiting one row's condition (at a given instance of it, where the row enumerates several) necessarily exhibits another's, the file is recorded against the narrower row, whose detector and detection point are the ones that apply. F1's front-block instance of F6 and its trailer-magic instance of F8, F35 of F36, L24 of L25, F21 of F22 and L10 of L11 stand in that relation; the property decides any pair and this list is not offered as closed.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both rows (F35 alone, or F35-and-F36 'both firing') resolve to the identical accept/reject verdict: reject-file / nonconforming. The disagreement is purely about register-row attribution for conformance-corpus bookkeeping, which does not change any implementation's accept/reject output or emitted bytes, so this is not byte-level divergent — but it is a genuine misreading by one walker of a rule stated identically, and correctly applied by the other walker, in both editions.

findings.title: Edition B's R-CNF-02 drops A's three named conduct-rule examples and its cross-reference sentence, but each example's own rule survives unchanged at its own section
findings.detail: Edition A's R-CNF-02 bullet names three illustrative writer-conduct-rule cases inline (a set ignore-lane bit, a pre-trailer gap longer than the commit protocol's pad, and §20.3 step 4's bar on changing a layer's fixed declarations) and closes with 'each is declared where it arises rather than enumerated here.' Edition B's R-CNF-02 bullet states only the general rule, with no illustrative list and no such cross-reference sentence. I checked each of the three examples at its own section in B: §6.3 still says a set ignore-lane bit 'is nevertheless not a file-conformance violation'; §6.2 still says a longer pre-trailer gap 'is conforming, though no conforming commit produces one'; §20.3 step 4 still says the bar on changing a layer's fixed declarations 'binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself.' All three are present, word for word or near-identically, in edition B at their own locations — only the aggregating illustrative list inside R-CNF-02 itself, and the 'declared where it arises' framing sentence, are gone. An implementer building a verifier from either edition's full text would reach the identical conclusion for all three scenarios.
findings.quotation_a: A few obligations this specification places on writers govern their conduct rather than their output... and a file is never nonconforming by virtue of one: conduct rules bind the actor, the predicate binds the bytes... §6.3's flags rules against a set ignore-lane bit..., §6.2's pre-trailer gap longer than [R-LIF-02] step 5's pad, and §20.3 step 4's bar on the fixed declarations of a layer that stores a tile are the cases this text states, and each is declared where it arises rather than enumerated here.
findings.quotation_b: A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer and never makes a file nonconforming.
findings.byte_level_rationale: No implementation built from B alone would reach a different per-scenario conclusion than one built from A alone: each of A's three named examples is independently and identically (or near-identically) restated at its own section in B, so the accept/reject outcome for every scenario the aggregating list covers is unchanged. The loss is confined to an expository cross-reference and illustrative list, not to any normative content a verifier implementation consults.

findings.title: B moves R-CNF-11's inline cannot-establish-grounds enumeration into §21.6's own closing paragraph, restated almost verbatim
findings.detail: Edition A's R-CNF-11 paragraph (§2.3) inlines the full list of cannot-establish grounds directly in the Conforming-verifier bullet: unimplemented format major, an unimplemented MU=1 top-level type, an unexecutable codec/filter, a declined layer/tile decode on resource grounds, a declined user-metadata-document decode, plus the experimental-range-encoding carve-out. Edition B's R-CNF-11 paragraph states only 'the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground (§21.6 names the grounds)' and defers to §21.6, whose own closing paragraph in B then states essentially the same list in essentially the same words ('A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports cannot establish ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter...'). I read both full passages in both editions and the content is the same grounds list, relocated and lightly compressed, not narrowed or widened.
findings.quotation_a: [cannot establish] ... the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground, as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.quotation_b: [cannot establish], the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground (§21.6 names the grounds). ... [§21.6:] A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports cannot establish ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: The same five grounds, in the same substance, govern cannot-establish in both editions; only their textual location (inline in R-CNF-11 vs. deferred to §21.6) differs, so no implementation built from one edition alone would recognize a ground, or fail to recognize one, that an implementation built from the other edition would treat differently.

findings.title: Both walks' ambiguity/observation findings (codec-incapable 'conforming verifier' status; unwitnessed cross-generation declaration changes) trace to text identical in both editions
findings.detail: Verifier-a's finding (verifiera-01) and verifier-b's finding (verifierb-01) are the same genuine ambiguity: whether software lacking a core/assigned codec or filter can be a 'conforming verifier' at all, given R-CNF-03's absolute, class-level 'no subset profiles' bar versus R-CNF-11/R-COD-11's apparently unconditional, file-by-file cannot-establish ground for an unexecutable codec. I read §2.3's Conforming-reader bullet (R-CNF-03) and §17.4's full R-COD-11 paragraph side by side in both editions and they are byte-identical (modulo two cosmetic punctuation substitutions). Likewise, verifier-b's second finding (verifierb-02, OBSERVATION, about cross-generation declaration changes being 'unwitnessed' to the verifier's live-state-only walk) has no separate Findings-section entry in verifier-a's transcript, but the identical substance (same quotations, same symptomatic-row list T2/T3/T4/T5/T14/T17/T21/T22/T24/T25, same §21.7 framing) is present inside verifier-a's own V5 answer. I read §21.7's full 'unwitnessed' definition and the symptomatic-row parenthetical in both editions and they are byte-identical. In both cases the underlying text each walker drew on is the same in A and B; the apparent divergence (two findings in B's transcript vs. one promoted finding plus the same material folded into a probe answer in A's transcript) is a difference in each walker's write-up choices, not a difference the rewrite introduced or removed.
findings.quotation_a: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file... For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]).
findings.quotation_b: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file... For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03]).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Since the governing passages are byte-identical between editions, an implementation built from A alone and one built from B alone face exactly the same unresolved ambiguity and exactly the same unwitnessed-condition limit; neither edition's rewrite created or closed either gap, so there is no edition-attributable byte-level divergence to report.

findings.title: Worked-example Note on the format-major "reach" test (F14/F5/F15) is dropped with no restatement
findings.detail: A's §2.3 ends with a Note that uses three concrete register rows — F14, F5 and F15 — to illustrate that a condition "reaches" a foreign format major because of the invariant it asserts, not the bytes it happens to read: F14 reaches despite checksumming redefinable trailer bytes, F5 does not reach despite its subject (file size) being non-redefinable, and F15 does not reach despite citing the same governing rule as F14. B keeps the general rule this Note illustrates (verbatim in substance, in §21.2's opening paragraph and in the §2.3-equivalent prose about `[R-CNF-13]`), but drops the Note itself entirely; an implementer reading B alone has to re-derive why F5 and F15 behave differently from F14 rather than being shown the worked contrast.
findings.quotation_a: §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only `[R-CNT-24]`'s CRC-32C at F − 4 over [F − 64, F − 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine... F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The register row list that actually decides which rows reach a foreign format major (F8, F14, F6, both of F1's instances, and no other row) is stated identically in both editions' §21.2; an implementation derives the same reach/no-reach verdict for F5, F14 and F15 from that list alone. The dropped Note only explains why, it does not change the verdict.

findings.title: Note on "reject" meaning scope-of-unusability rather than UI is dropped with no restatement
findings.detail: A closes §2.4 with a one-sentence Note clarifying that the register's "reject" vocabulary prescribes which scope becomes unusable, not how an implementation surfaces that to a user or caller. B's §21 and §2.4 never restate this distinction anywhere; checked by grepping both files for the Note's distinctive phrases.
findings.quotation_a: "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is a clarification about reporting/UI, explicitly outside the bytes-and-behavior scope the rest of the document's requirements govern; its absence changes no MUST/SHOULD rule and so no implementation's accept/reject behavior or emitted bytes.

findings.title: Sentence tying preserve-verbatim to reader outcomes as orthogonal is dropped
findings.detail: A's §2.4 states explicitly that the ignore-record outcome and the preserve-verbatim updater obligation are orthogonal — a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater must preserve — right after noting that the "ignore" vocabulary is reused for defined non-violations. B drops this connecting sentence; its §2.4 still carries a preserve-verbatim table row (pointing to §20.4) and the outcome-class table, from which the same fact is derivable by a reader who checks both, but the document no longer states the relationship directly.
findings.quotation_a: The same vocabulary is used for defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is *ignored*, not rejected). **preserve-verbatim** names an updater obligation, orthogonal to reader outcomes: a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves.
findings.quotation_b: Every detectable file-conformance violation named by this specification is assigned exactly one **reader outcome**: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record. `[R-CNF-07]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: §20.4's table (identical in both editions) already states which records an updater must preserve regardless of whether a reader ignores them; the dropped sentence is an explanatory bridge between two unchanged rules, not a rule change itself.

findings.title: Entire §3.3 subsection — the Part I/Part II independence claim load-bearing for §7 and §20 — has no counterpart in B
findings.detail: A's §3.3 consists of one Note stating that Part I (the container) is independent of Part II (the array model) by construction, so appenders and rewriters can carry a layer forward without being able to decode it — and the Note explicitly flags this independence as load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20. B has no §3.3 at all (its §3 ends after §3.2, "The reference array"), and I confirmed by grep across the whole of ed_b.md that no sentence anywhere restates the independence claim, including inside §7 and §20 themselves, which I reread in full.
findings.quotation_a: Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Every specific rule this claim explains (an appender copying an unrecognized record's extent without decoding it, a rewriter relocating a tile index without decoding tile payloads) is independently stated with its own MUST/MUST NOT language in §7.2 and §20.1-§20.5, unchanged between editions; the dropped passage is the architectural justification for why those rules can coexist, not an additional rule, so an implementation follows the same bytes-level obligations either way.

findings.title: Note distinguishing general bit-numbering (R-ENC-08) from §14's boolean-sample-to-bit mapping is dropped
findings.detail: A's §4.4 closes with a short Note warning that the bit-0-is-LSB rule it just stated is the general flags/packed-field rule, and that the separate question of how boolean *samples* map to bits is answered in §14, not here. B drops this Note with no restatement; `[R-ENC-08]` (the rule it annotates) is cited nowhere else in either edition, so no other passage's correctness depends on this specific clarification, but a reader of B alone loses the explicit pointer distinguishing the two rules.
findings.quotation_a: This rule fixes bit numbering in flags and packed fields generally; the mapping of boolean *samples* to bits is defined in §14.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: §14.3's packed-boolean-plane rules state their own bit-k-of-byte-k-div-8 mapping independently and completely in both editions; the dropped Note was only a navigational pointer between two already-separate, already-complete rule statements.

findings.title: Half of the layout-table Note is dropped: the "name is structural" classification and two documentation-method claims
findings.detail: A's §4.7 Note, after explaining what a layout table's columns carry, adds three further claims: that a name is itself a structural field (citing the specific duplicate-name violation rows F4/L9), that every non-obvious encoding in the document is followed by a worked numeric example, and that every sentinel or overloaded encoding additionally has a paired conformance vector, plus that all named constants appear once in Appendix B. B's rewritten Note covers only the first half (what the columns mean) and ends there; none of the second half's four claims is restated anywhere else in B.
findings.quotation_a: A name is structural: a duplicate is a validity error at file or layer scope (`[R-ENC-15]`, F4, L9), and its length prefix is §7.4's framing, not its value. Every non-obvious encoding is followed by a worked numeric example, and every sentinel or overloaded encoding additionally has a paired conformance vector. All named constants appear once in Appendix B.
findings.quotation_b: §7.2's table folds a field's range into its Field cell where it states one, and the field's remaining bounds are stated in the rules below the table.
findings.byte_level_rationale: The duplicate-layer-name violation itself (F4) is registered, identically worded, in §21.2 of both editions regardless of whether §4.7 separately calls names "structural"; the worked-example/conformance-vector and Appendix-B claims are statements about the document's own authoring conventions, not requirements on an implementation's bytes or behavior.

findings.title: The claim that Part I alone yields a working container reader, with Part II needed only for sample values, is dropped from the introduction with no restatement
findings.detail: A's §1 closes by telling the reader that Part I (§5–§10) alone yields a container reader that can open files, walk the directory and list layers without decoding a single sample, and that returning actual sample values additionally needs Part II, because §19.3's layer-access validation resolves into Part II's value-set and geometry rules. B's rewritten "How to read this document" paragraph describes the document's rubric (purpose/layout-table/writer-rules/reader-rules/worked-examples) and the structural/descriptive field classification instead, and never restates the Part I/Part II capability-split claim anywhere in B.
findings.quotation_a: Part I alone yields a container reader — one that opens files, walks the directory, and lists layers without decoding a sample; returning sample values needs Part II as well, since §19.3's layer validation resolves into Part II's value sets and geometry rules at every step.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: §1 is expressly excluded from this document's normative text by `[R-CNF-01]` in both editions, and the claim is an architectural orientation remark, not a rule; §19.1-§19.4's actual open/access/read algorithms, which this remark summarizes, are unchanged between editions.

findings.location_a: Front matter, Note before §1 (outside any numbered section)
findings.title: The claim that test vectors cite requirement identifiers rather than prose positions is dropped when the front-matter Note is folded into §1
findings.detail: A's document opens (before "### 1. Introduction") with a Note on how to read the document, most of which B preserves by moving it into ordinary (non-Note) prose inside §1 itself. One clause of that Note is not carried over anywhere: that normative requirements carry stable identifiers and that test vectors cite those identifiers rather than citing prose positions in the document. B's §2.2 states the general stable-identifier rule (identical in both editions) but never states the specific claim that test vectors key off identifiers rather than prose position.
findings.quotation_a: Normative requirements carry stable identifiers like `[R-IDX-03]`, and test vectors cite those identifiers rather than prose positions.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: §24's conformance-vector manifest format (identical in both editions) already requires each vector's manifest entry to record the §21 register row and its governing requirement identifier, which is the operative mechanism this dropped sentence was describing; its absence from the introduction does not change what a vector manifest actually records.

findings.title: B drops A's clarification that ignore-record also covers non-violations and preserve-verbatim is orthogonal to reader outcomes
findings.detail: A's §2.4, right after defining the reader-outcome vocabulary (reject-file/reject-layer/reject-tile/ignore-record) and before the outcome table, states two general points: (1) the same 'ignore-record'/'ignored' vocabulary is also used for defined conditions that are not violations at all (its own example: an unknown ancillary record is ignored, not rejected); and (2) preserve-verbatim names an updater obligation that is orthogonal to reader outcomes — a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater is obliged to preserve verbatim. B's §2.4 goes straight from the R-CNF-07 citation into the outcome table, omitting both sentences. B's own preserve-verbatim table row ('Binds updaters: the bytes are carried forward unmodified...') states only the updater-binding half, never the orthogonality-to-reader-outcomes half. I confirmed by grep that no other section of B restates this general principle (searched 'orthogonal to reader', 'ignored, not rejected', 'is ignored, not' — all zero hits); B's §21.6 table does use 'Ignored' language for several non-violation rows, so the practice is exhibited by example, but the explicit general rule connecting that usage to §2.4's outcome-class vocabulary, and the explicit statement that an ignored record can still be a preserved one, is stated only in A. An implementer who read only B's §2.4 and the preserve-verbatim table row could reasonably (and wrongly) infer that 'ignore-record' denotes only a violation-outcome parallel to reject-file/layer/tile, or fail to realize that a reader's decision to ignore an unimplemented ancillary record says nothing about an updater's independent obligation to carry that same record's bytes forward unmodified under §20.4's PE-bit table — a divergence that could change what bytes an updater emits.
findings.quotation_a: The same vocabulary is used for defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is *ignored*, not rejected). **preserve-verbatim** names an updater obligation, orthogonal to reader outcomes: a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: An updater implementation built from B's §2.4 alone, without separately deriving the point from §20.4's PE-bit table (which does state the preservation rule but never ties it back to §2.4's 'ignore-record' label or flags the orthogonality), risks treating a reader-ignored record as safe to drop rather than preserve, producing a directory that drops a record §20.4's MU=0/PE=1 row requires it to retain byte-identically — a different set of bytes in the output directory than an implementation built from A, which states the orthogonality as a standalone rule impossible to miss in §2.4 itself.

findings.location_a: §2.4 Outcome classes and owning scope (closing Note)
findings.title: B drops A's Note distinguishing the Reject outcome classes from implementation/reporting technique
findings.detail: A closes §2.4 with a short Note: 'Reject' prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique. This has no counterpart anywhere in B (the only hit for 'implementation technique' in B, §2.1's Note, is about requirement-phrasing discipline in general, not this specific point). The Note is explanatory rather than a rule: nothing in either edition prescribes how a reader signals rejection to its caller, so dropping the Note does not change what any conforming implementation must do — it only removes a reminder against a misreading no normative text in either edition invites. Reported as an observation rather than a LOSS because no byte or verdict differs between an implementation built from A versus B on this point.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Neither edition's normative text constrains error-reporting mechanism/UI; the Note only forecloses a misreading, so an implementation built from B alone has the same freedom (by silence) that A grants explicitly, and no byte or accept/reject verdict differs.

findings.title: A's glossary defines "addressed" layer-wide; B's defines it generation-relative
findings.detail: A's glossary entry says simply 'every tile of a layer is addressed,' a layer-wide, generation-invariant statement. B's glossary entry instead says a tile 'is addressed in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15).' Both editions' main normative bodies agree a dimension's extent MAY grow (and MUST NOT shrink) across generations (§20.3), which means the set of tiles belonging to a layer's grid can itself grow between generations — making B's generation-qualified wording the technically correct one and A's unqualified wording the looser one. Neither edition's normative rules outside the glossary turn on the glossary's own phrasing (the real rule lives in §11.1/§11.2/§15/§20.3, identically in both editions), so this is reported as an ambiguity/precision difference in the informal glossary text, not a decided-content LOSS or ADDITION.
findings.quotation_a: **addressed tile / stored tile** — every tile of a layer is *addressed*.
findings.quotation_b: a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions' operative rules (§11.1 geometry, §15 tile index, §20.3 extent growth) are identical in substance in A and B; an implementer who read past the glossary into the normative sections would build the same addressed-tile logic from either edition. The difference is confined to the informal definition's precision, not to a decided rule.

findings.location_a: §2.4 Outcome classes and owning scope (paragraph following the reader-outcome enumeration)
findings.title: B drops the sentence pair on non-violation ignore-record vocabulary and preserve-verbatim's orthogonality to reader outcomes
findings.detail: A states, right after naming the four reader outcomes under [R-CNF-07]: that the same outcome vocabulary also names defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is ignored, not rejected), and that preserve-verbatim is an updater obligation orthogonal to reader outcomes -- a record a reader is permitted to ignore can still be one an updater is bound to carry forward byte-identically. B's §2.4 stops at the [R-CNF-07] citation and never states either clause anywhere else in the document (checked by grepping 'orthogonal' and 'ignored, not rejected' across all of B: zero hits; the same searches against A return exactly these lines, proving the search methodology). An implementer building from B alone would still reach the correct updater behavior, because §20.4's preservation table (identical in both editions) keys the obligation purely to the stored MU/PE flags, never to what a reader does with the record, and §21.6's table already uses the word 'Ignored' for non-violations without needing §2.4's permission to reuse it. So the rule survives operationally in both editions; only this explanatory bridge sentence, which a careful reader of A would use to understand *why* the vocabulary and the updater obligation don't conflict, is missing from B.
findings.quotation_a: Every detectable file-conformance violation named by this specification is assigned exactly one **reader outcome**: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record. `[R-CNF-07]` The same vocabulary is used for defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is *ignored*, not rejected). **preserve-verbatim** names an updater obligation, orthogonal to reader outcomes: a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves.
findings.quotation_b: Every detectable file-conformance violation named by this specification is assigned exactly one **reader outcome**: reject-file, reject-layer, reject-tile, or ignore-record. `[R-CNF-07]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: No construction forces a different byte or verdict: §20.4's MU/PE-keyed preservation table and §21.6's own 'Ignored' language are unchanged, word-for-word, in both editions and are self-sufficient without this bridging sentence. Verified by reading §20.4 and §21.6 in full in both editions (see transcript method step 5 and rejected candidate 1).

findings.location_a: §2.4 Outcome classes and owning scope, closing Note
findings.title: B drops §2.4's closing Note that 'reject' names a scope of unusability, not a user-interface requirement
findings.detail: A closes §2.4 with a Note clarifying that the word 'reject' in this specification's outcome vocabulary prescribes which scope of the file becomes unusable, not how a conforming implementation must surface that fact to a user -- i.e. it does not mandate any particular error message or UI. B's §2.4 ends one paragraph earlier, at [R-CNF-12], and proceeds straight to §2.5; grepping 'not user interface' and 'prescribes the scope' across all of B returns zero hits. Because the dropped text was itself inside a Note in A, it was already non-normative under [R-CNF-01] (text labelled Note, Example, or Rationale is excluded from this document's normative text), so no implementation behavior in either edition turns on it.
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The dropped text was itself a Note, explicitly non-normative in A under [R-CNF-01]; its removal cannot change what either edition requires a reader, writer, updater, or verifier to do with any byte.

findings.title: All of A's §3.3, a Note on Part I/Part II independence being load-bearing for the updater rules, is missing from B
findings.detail: A has a one-paragraph subsection, 3.3, consisting of a Note stating that Part I (the container) is independent of Part II (the array model) by construction -- no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads -- so that appenders and rewriters carrying a layer forward can operate on files whose layers they cannot decode, and that this independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20. A subsection-number diff across every '####' heading in both documents found this is the only N.N subsection present in A with no counterpart in B; the other 92 subsections in each document line up one-to-one. Grepping the distinctive phrases 'Container and array model', 'independent of Part II', 'carry a layer forward', and 'cannot decode' across all of B returns zero hits for every one of the four; the same four searches against A return exactly the quoted Note, proving the searches work. B goes directly from §3.2 (The reference array) to §2 (Conformance, which in B's reordering follows §3).
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The dropped text is a Note, non-normative under [R-CNF-01] even in A. The architectural property it describes is still true of, and still exercised by, both editions' unchanged §7 and §20 rules (an appender's and a rewriter's writer obligations run only to bytes, never to decoded content, e.g. [R-WRT-01], [R-WRT-05]) -- confirmed identical in both editions during the §20.3/20.4/20.5 comparison in method step 5.

findings.title: No outcome class is stated for a reader lacking an assigned core codec/filter it is obliged to implement
findings.detail: R-CNF-03 declares software that cannot execute an assigned core codec/filter (e.g. zstd) non-conforming, but the document never states what such software's behavior is. §17.4's reject-layer treatment is grammatically confined to a conforming reader meeting a reserved/experimental codec value, not an assigned one it simply hasn't implemented. §21.9/R-ERR-04's resource-decline mechanism is scoped to the limits table's named quantities (rank, channels, entry_count, layers, dir_length, tile size, metadata size, zstd window) and never mentions codec/filter capability. §21.6's closing paragraph names exactly two 'conforming files a reader nevertheless refuses' (unimplemented format major; experimental-range top-level MU=1 type) and does not include this case. An implementer shipping a reader without zstd support gets no guidance on whether to refuse the whole file, reject only the layer, or serve the layer's declarations while refusing only its tile reads — all three are equally consistent with the text, since none of the three is a 'conforming reader' to begin with and no further constraint distinguishes them.
findings.quotation_a: "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Two implementations built from this text alone, each omitting zstd, can diverge on which bytes they will emit/accept from a file whose only defect (from their point of view) is a zstd-coded layer: one refuses the whole file (no bytes served from any layer), another serves every other layer and refuses only the zstd layer's tile reads, a third serves even that layer's name/geometry/channel declarations while refusing only sample data. All three satisfy every sentence the document states, so resolving the gap would change which of these three behaviors is sanctioned.

findings.title: Probe R4's field names (extent_offset/extent_length) do not match the document's tile-index-entry field names (offset/length)
findings.detail: This is not a defect in edition A; it is a note on the probe's own wording. The document's tile-index entry (§15.1) has fields named 'offset' and 'length'; 'extent_offset'/'extent_length' is the document's name for a different structure at a different scope — a record's extent slot (§7.2), which is never tested against the all-ones sentinel anywhere in the text. Read charitably as referring to the entry's offset/length fields, the condition in probe R4 maps cleanly onto register row T7. Flagged for transparency since a comparison across implementers answering the same probe from different texts could otherwise be thrown off by this naming mismatch, not because edition A itself is unclear.
findings.quotation_a: "0 | 8 | u64 | offset | structural | see §15.3 | 8 | 8 | u64 | length | structural | see §15.3" (§15.1 entry layout table)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is a terminology note about the probe's phrasing, not a claim that two implementations built from edition A alone would diverge on any byte — the document itself is internally consistent and unambiguous once the correct field names are substituted.

findings.title: No outcome class or register row for software that cannot execute a core, assigned codec or filter
findings.detail: The document mandates that every conforming reader implement all four assigned codecs and both assigned filters (they are core, with 'no subset profiles'); R-CNF-03 and R-COD-11 state that software failing this is categorically 'not a conforming reader,' but neither they nor §21's register assign that software an outcome class or behavior when it meets a layer validly declaring one of those assigned, core values anyway. Contrast the fully specified, adjacent case: a reserved or experimental codec value is a plain value-set violation under R-COD-03, register row L43, pinned to reject-layer with the layer's name still listable and every other layer unaffected. Concretely: a layer validly declares codec = 3 (zstd, assigned and core per §10.2). Implementation A, lacking a zstd decoder, treats this as reject-layer and serves the file's other layers; Implementation B treats it as reject-file and refuses the whole file; Implementation C returns zero-filled or garbage bytes for the layer's tiles. All three are equally consistent with R-CNF-03/R-COD-11's silence, which states only that the software itself falls outside the conformance classes — it supplies no bytes-level test by which one choice is correct and the others are not, because by its own framing the software making the choice has already left the set of actors the conformance classes govern. A second implementer answering this round's R3 from a different edition therefore has no textual anchor to converge on beyond 'such software is nonconforming,' and the two implementers' answers for what that software actually does can diverge arbitrarily while both remain faithful readings.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST... handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core... There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.
findings.quotation_b: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving the ambiguity changes which bytes such software may serve for the affected layer (fill values from reject-layer treatment, nothing at all from reject-file treatment, or raw/garbage decoded bytes from a 'best effort' treatment) and whether it may continue to serve every other layer in the file; the document supplies no comparison, checksum, or value-set test that selects among these, since the actor facing the choice is defined to be outside the reader conformance classes entirely.

findings.location_a: §20.3 step 4 ('the fixed declarations' / 'what the line gives up' / 'no check any actor owes able to see it' passage); [R-CNF-02]
findings.title: A fill-value-only change on a layer with no edge padding leaves no file-conformance witness, though the act is barred as conduct
findings.detail: §20.3 step 4 bars an appender from changing a stored-tile layer's fill value (among other fixed declarations); [R-CNF-02] explicitly classifies this bar as a conduct rule rather than a file-conformance predicate, and §20.3 step 4 itself narrows the independent witnesses of such a change to a short named list of register rows (T2-T5, T14, T17, T21-T25) plus outright decode/framing failure -- all of which require the layer to have edge-tile padding (§11.3) or a codec/filter change to fire. A writer implementing only the structural checks this specification obliges would, for a layer whose extent is an exact multiple of its tile extent (no edge padding), see a resulting file pass every §21 check and be certified conforming by a verifier, even though the writer that produced it violated the bound conduct rule. An implementer relying on 'the file will be rejected if I get this wrong' would be surprised: for the common case of evenly-tiled layers, nothing rejects it.
findings.quotation_a: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself ... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out. ... but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7).
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It determines, for the common case of a layer with no edge padding, which bytes a conforming verifier is obliged to accept and certify: a file produced by an impermissible fill-only commit and a file produced by a permissible one (same resulting bytes) are both certifiable as conforming, since no listed check fires. This is not a disagreement between two passages of the document -- it is the document's own explicit, self-consistent statement of a byte-level consequence that an implementer building only from the 'MUST NOT' sentence in §20.3 step 4 could easily miss without also reading [R-CNF-02] and §21.7's enumeration.

findings.title: A creator that decodes an input file and re-emits it drops ignore-lane bits an appender/rewriter would keep
findings.detail: An appender and a rewriter are both bound to copy forward unknown ignore-lane bits of their input unchanged (§6.3's [R-CNT-08]; §20.3 step 6; §20.5's [R-WRT-06]-adjacent text). A plain creator owes its input nothing at all, even one whose only input is the fully-decoded content of an existing TARN file: §20.1 states 'As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read... it writes flags = 0,' and §6.3 independently requires flags = 0 of any writer creating a file under this text. The tier distinction is keyed only to whether the output extends the input file under the same file_id, never to whether the writer happened to read that input first. A tool that reads a TARN file, decodes everything it understands, and writes a logically equivalent new file (rather than appending, or rewriting under §20.5's fresh-file_id procedure) is a creator, and silently loses any feature signalled only by a later-minor ignore-lane bit, with no MUST to report the loss and no register row recording it.
findings.quotation_a: As a creator it undertakes nothing toward its input, whatever it read: §20.2 binds it, it writes flags = 0
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving which tier a decode-then-recreate tool occupies changes the literal trailer bytes it must emit at the flags field — zero versus carrying bit 20 forward — and the document resolves it unambiguously to zero, a real, citable, byte-level consequence even though it is not an indeterminacy in the text.

findings.title: A fill-only change to a stored layer's conformance outcome turns entirely on whether any of its stored tiles has a padding position
findings.detail: §20.3 bars a commit from changing a stored layer's fill value, but states the bar 'binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms.' Working the fill-only case through the document's own witness list, the only check that can possibly fire is T4 (padding content, [R-SER-05]), and T4 has nothing to examine unless some stored tile of that layer actually has a padding position (an edge tile under §11.3/[R-GEO-04]). A layer whose every dimension's extent is an exact multiple of its tile extent has no padding anywhere, so a conduct-violating fill-only edit to such a layer can leave a file no stated verifier check anywhere in the document distinguishes from a conforming one — the writer broke a MUST, yet the resulting bytes pass every rule the document states.
findings.quotation_a: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Whether a verifier may certify the resulting file turns exactly on a literal, checkable fact about the edited layer's stored bytes — whether any stored tile has a padding position — which is precisely the condition T4 examines; for a padding-free layer no stated check rejects the file despite the writer-conduct violation, a determinate but easily-missed byte-level outcome.

findings.location_a: §15.1 (tile-index region and entry layout), the region-layout diagram
findings.title: §15.1's tile-index region layout is the document's one unlabeled blockquote, and is therefore fully normative despite looking like an aside
findings.detail: `[R-CNF-01]` makes a blockquote non-normative only when labeled Note, Example, or Rationale; an unlabeled one is normative. Scanning every blockquote in the document for its leading label, exactly one carries none: the §15.1 statement that the tile-index region is, contiguously, an entry array followed by a segment-CRC array, with no padding anywhere inside the region. Every other blockquote in the document is a Note, an Example, or a Rationale. This one clause is fully binding, and [R-CNT-17]'s extent_length formula and [R-IDX-01]'s per-entry offset rule (entry k at region byte 20·k) both silently presuppose exactly this ordering and the absence of internal padding. An implementer applying a surface heuristic of 'blockquote formatting means aside, skip it' instead of checking the label, which is exactly the mistake `[R-CNF-01]`'s own phrasing is written to prevent, would miss that this is the one place the region's internal byte ordering is actually stated.
findings.quotation_a: the tile-index region addressed by the layer record's extent slot is, contiguously: [ entry array: entry_count × 20 bytes ] [ segment CRC array: ⌈entry_count / 2¹⁶⌉ × 4 bytes ]
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: If this clause were mistakenly treated as illustrative, an implementation could accept a tile-index region with the segment-CRC array placed before the entry array or with padding inserted between them, producing disagreement with another implementation about where entry k's 20 bytes actually sit, even though every other stated rule (the per-entry offset formula, the extent_length cross-check) would still nominally apply; the document's own labeling convention is exactly what forecloses that divergence, which is why the missing label on an otherwise-normative passage is worth flagging.

findings.title: R-CNF-11's unqualified 'cannot execute a codec or filter' ground for cannot-establish is not reconciled with R-CNF-03's blanket, class-level disqualification
findings.detail: R-CNF-11 (§2.3) names, as a standing ground for the cannot-establish verdict, 'when it cannot execute a codec or filter (R-COD-11)' with no restriction to reserved/experimental values. Read alone, this licenses any verifier — including one missing a core codec such as zstd or lz4 — to report cannot-establish layer-by-layer while otherwise certifying files that do not use the missing codec, remaining a 'conforming verifier' throughout. But R-CNF-03 (§2.3) states, with no per-file qualifier, that 'software that declines to support a core codec... is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly,' and verifiers 'inherit every reader obligation' (§2.3). R-COD-11's own second sentence (§17.4) then narrows the only circumstance in which an actually-conforming reader can be in the 'cannot execute' position at all to a reserved or experimental codec/filter value, since every assigned one is core. The document never rewrites R-CNF-11's phrasing to reflect that narrowing, so an implementer reading R-CNF-11 in isolation is not told whether a verifier lacking a core codec may still legitimately certify other files under the conforming-verifier label (reading a) or is disqualified from that class for every file it processes (reading b).
findings.quotation_a: "There are no subset profiles: software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly." (R-CNF-03) vs. "...when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11])..." (R-CNF-11, §2.3) vs. "For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer ([R-COD-03], [R-COD-09]); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader ([R-CNF-03])." (R-COD-11, §17.4)
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Under reading (a) a verifier missing a core codec may certify, as conforming, files that only use codecs it does support; under reading (b) that same software is disqualified from the conforming-verifier/conforming-reader class entirely, and none of its accept/reject outputs — for any file, including ones that never touch the missing codec — count as a conforming verifier's verdicts under this specification. That is a direct disagreement about which files an implementation may validly certify and under what label, not merely a difference in how a result is phrased.

findings.title: Undetermined whether codec-incapable software is ever a 'conforming verifier' at all
findings.detail: R-CNF-03 states an absolute, exception-free bar: 'MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core... There are no subset profiles: software that declines any of those is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly.' R-CNF-11 says a (conforming) verifier 'inherits every reader obligation,' which on its face includes this one unconditionally. Yet R-COD-11 and §21.6 both describe 'a verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter' as ordinary, licensed behavior that produces a defined report ('cannot establish'), using the very three-verdict vocabulary §2.3 reserves for the 'conforming verifier' class. An implementer building a verifier that is missing, say, an lz4 decoder must decide: (a) such software fails R-CNF-03's bar and is therefore not a conforming reader/verifier at all, so none of its output (for any file, not just lz4 ones) carries the normative weight of a certification; or (b) R-COD-11 implicitly carves out codec/filter execution as a capability ground on par with an unimplemented format major (whose non-support R-CNF-03 explicitly scopes as acceptable: 'every conforming file of a format major version it implements'), letting such software still issue valid cannot-establish verdicts for the affected layers while fully certifying others. The document never states which reading governs.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: A verifier that cannot execute a layer's codec or filter cannot establish that layer's conformance and MUST NOT certify the file. [...] For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03).
findings.byte_level_rationale: An implementer built from reading (b) alone produces software that, on meeting an unsupported-but-assigned codec, issues a 'cannot establish' report for just that layer and proceeds to fully certify the rest of the file (accepting/rejecting other layers' bytes on their own merits). An implementer built from reading (a) alone produces software that, on the same file, refuses to issue any verdict at all (since it holds itself disqualified from the verifier class the moment it lacks a core codec), and a pipeline consuming its output would have to treat every one of its reports -- including ones about files using only codec 1 -- as having no standing. The two implementations therefore accept/report differently on the identical byte stream whenever a core codec is unavailable to them, which is exactly the byte-level test: does resolving the ambiguity change what a conforming implementation may emit, or must accept or reject? Here it changes what the tool is entitled to assert at all.

findings.title: Cross-generation declaration changes are explicitly, by design, invisible to the verifier's live-state walk
findings.detail: §20.3 bars a commit from changing a fixed declaration of a layer that stored a tile, but states plainly that this bar binds the commit only as a writer-conduct rule: 'no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself.' §9.7 and its closing Note confirm the verifier's coverage walk only ever reaches the live trailer/directory and never reconstructs history. §21.7 names this the 'unwitnessed' category and gives the specific, narrow list of symptomatic rows (T2, T3, T4, T5, T14, T17, T21, T22, T24, T25) through which such a change can incidentally surface -- but only as an ordinary tile-scope finding, never attributed to its true cause. This is not a flaw I am alleging (the document states it as deliberate design, repeatedly and explicitly), but it is a real limit on what a 'conforming verifier' certifies: certification never implies that a layer's current declarations are consistent with what any earlier generation stored under the same layer, only that the live state as given is internally sound.
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself, the register enumerating file-conformance violations (§21.1) and the bar stating no condition a file can exhibit (§21.7, R-ERR-01, R-CNF-02)
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is a documented design limit, not an underdetermination: resolving it changes nothing about which bytes any conforming implementation may emit or must accept/reject, since the document is explicit and internally consistent about exactly this behavior; I report it as context an implementer should have, not as a gap needing a byte-level resolution.

result.notes: Working transcript with full section-by-section verification quotes, line numbers, and rationale for every group is at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-robertkleffner-Documents-GitHub-tarn-first-draft/fidelity-4/triage-implementer/transcript-triage-implementer.md (also kept in my scratch dir at .../fidelity-4/scratch/triage/transcript-triage-implementer.md). Lens applied throughout: implementer consequence — for every group I asked whether a builder working from edition B alone would emit a different byte, accept/reject a different file, or write a different branch than a builder working from edition A alone. Headline result: of 21 distinct differences/defects covering the 38 reports, zero are byte-level A-vs-B divergences. Several reports (G1, G2, G3) describe real, serious ambiguities or implementer traps — but every one of them is edition-invariant: the controlling text is byte-identical in A and B, so the defect (real as it is) belongs to the shared specification, not to B's translation of A, and I graded those EQUIVALENT rather than LOSS/AMBIGUITY for fidelity purposes while flagging them for a separate maintainer ticket. The genuine LOSSes (G4-G11) are all explanatory Notes, asides, or cross-reference sentences whose operative content is independently and completely restated elsewhere, unchanged, in both editions; none change a byte. I disagreed with one reporter's severity: swba-01's byte-level claim (group G6) does not survive direct inspection of §20.4's preservation table, which is self-contained and unchanged between editions. One reporter's REPORTER_ERROR characterization (cmp-verifier-01, group G13) and one OBSERVATION (readera-02, group G21) were confirmed correct on direct re-reading. Two reporters' AMBIGUITY grade (swba-03's glossary finding, group G12) was downgraded to EQUIVALENT since the glossary entry carries no requirement ID and the operative normative sections are unchanged and decide the question identically in both editions.

result.disclosure: A relayed "user request" (the single word "Go") was prepended above this computed brief by the harness; per the brief's own instruction this is the launcher's message to the orchestrator, carried out before this triage pass was spawned, is not a task for this pass, needs no reconciliation with the brief, and does not widen the access rule — disclosed once and not otherwise acted on. Access was limited to the two named edition files and the named transcript glob (opened by exact name; no directory was listed). All 38 findings were deduplicated into 21 groups covering every input id exactly once; each group's cited passages were independently re-read in both editions via grep/sed (with a control search proving zero-hit methodology whenever a dropped phrase was searched for) before grading. Full working log, including every passage checked and every quotation behind each grade, is at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-robertkleffner-Documents-GitHub-tarn-first-draft/fidelity-4/triage-skeptic/transcript-triage-skeptic.md.

2. I checked whether anything else in A cross-references §3.3 by number (`grep -n "§3\.3"` against all of A): zero hits. 3. Most importantly, I located the actual normative mechanism the Note is explaining — the rule that an appender/rewriter's obligations toward carried-forward structures stop short of decoding — and found it stated with full `[R-WRT-09]` force in **both** editions, in nearly identical language:

The claim is that A's §2.3 closing Note — which uses F14 (reaches despite checksumming redefinable bytes), F5 (does not reach despite a non-redefinable subject) and F15 (does not reach despite citing the same governing rule as F14) to illustrate the reach test — is dropped from B with "no restatement," leaving an implementer to re-derive the F5/F15 contrast alone.

I confirmed the Note's specific wording is indeed absent from B: a direct search for its distinctive phrases ("trailer bytes it requires be zero", "128-byte floor" in the F5 context, "three rows show"/"carries the weight") returns zero hits in spec/tarn.md, including a whitespace-normalized search to defeat the hard wrap, and a control search for a phrase known to be present ("128-byte floor" occurs once, elsewhere, at a different point, §9-ish on extent slack — proving the search mechanism itself works and isn't swallowing matches).

But the question for a loss-refuter is not whether the Note's *prose* survives — it doesn't — but whether what it *decides* survives elsewhere in B, such that an implementation built from B alone reaches the same verdict as one built from A. It does, via three passages B keeps, each matching A's corresponding (non-Note) prose in substance:

1. B §2.3 states the same general test A states outside its Note: the property violated, not the bytes read, decides reach, and explicitly allows a check to read redefinable bytes while asserting a fixed property — the exact shape of the F14 case.
2. B §6.3's `[R-CNT-24]` states that only "the remaining 48 trailer bytes" (i.e., bytes outside the permanently-fixed magic/version/CRC fields) may be redefined by a future major. F15's subject — the 12 reserved bytes at trailer offset 48–60 — falls inside that redefinable 48, which is exactly A's Note's stated reason F15 doesn't reach even though its Governing-rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`.
3. Decisively, B's §21.2 opening paragraph keeps, essentially verbatim, A's own non-Note sentence: "Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances, each asserting an invariant `[R-CNT-24]` fixes in every major, and no other row." This sentence is the operative enumeration: it affirmatively states which of §21.2's 35 conditions reach (F14 among them) and which do not ("no other row" — which excludes F5 and F15 by name, since they are two of the 35 rows and are not in the "yields" set). This sentence exists in A outside the Note (lines 3838–3841) and is carried into B almost unchanged (lines 3629–3634; only the em-dash punctuation was spruced to commas), so it was never something the Note alone supplied — the Note explained *why* this enumeration comes out the way it does for three rows chosen as illustration; it added no additional fact to the enumeration itself.

Applying the byte-level test: an implementer who has B's §2.3 test, B's §6.3 `[R-CNT-24]` byte-range split, and B's §21.2 "yields ... and no other row" sentence can determine, for F14, F5 and F15 alike, exactly the same accept/reject-relevant reach/no-reach status that A's Note illustrates — because that status is literally named in the enumeration sentence, and the *reason* (property-vs-bytes, and which 48 bytes are redefinable) is available from the two rule statements that are substantively identical across editions. No byte emitted or verdict reached by a reader or verifier built from B differs from one built from A on this account. What's missing is pedagogy — a worked walk-through naming the three rows and spelling out the "despite"/"although" contrast — not a decision. That differs from the implementer pass's own conclusion (which conceded the §21.2 sentence "alone, unchanged, determines the reach/no-reach verdict... including F5, F14 and F15" yet still graded LOSS): if the sentence already determines the verdict without the Note, the Note is not decisive, and its loss cannot fail the byte-level test the brief sets as the actual standard.

I therefore refute the LOSS classification: the figure's conclusions, not just the general rule, are already fully recoverable from B's own stated text.

result.decisive_quotes:
A, §2.3 closing Note (lines 283–294):
"> **Note.** The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only `[R-CNT-24]`'s CRC-32C at F − 4 over [F − 64, F − 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F (`[R-CNT-27]`), and those are format major 1's. F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine."

A, §21.2 opening paragraph (lines 3836–3841), present outside the Note:
"Which rows reach a file declaring a format major other than 1 is decided by `[R-CNF-13]` (§2.3), condition by condition. Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances — each asserting an invariant `[R-CNT-24]` fixes in every major — and no other row."

B, §2.3 closing paragraph (lines 269–276):
"A condition **reaches** a file declaring a format major other than 1 when, and only when, the property it violates is one `[R-CNT-24]` fixes for every format major version. What matters is the property a check asserts, not the bytes it reads: a check can read bytes a future major is free to redefine and still assert only a property fixed for every major."

B, §6.3, `[R-CNT-24]` paragraph (lines 757–761):
"In every format major version, the following are permanently fixed: the final 64 bytes of a file contain the trailer magic at F − 64, version_major and version_minor at F − 56, and a CRC-32C at F − 4 covering bytes [F − 64, F − 4); and the front signature block (§6.1) is constant. A future major MAY redefine only the remaining 48 trailer bytes and MUST NOT grow the trailer; additional space comes from structures placed before it."

B, §21.2 opening paragraph (lines 3629–3634):
"Which rows reach a file declaring a format major other than 1 is decided by `[R-CNF-13]` (§2.3), condition by condition. Deriving it there yields F8, F14, F6 and both of F1's instances, each asserting an invariant `[R-CNT-24]` fixes in every major, and no other row."
